pages.title: M365 Setup & File Organization Guide
pages.html:
There are a few things worth setting up once, at the start, so that turning in written work later is simple. This page stays available all year. Come back to it whenever you need it.

Signing in to Microsoft 365

Your school gives you a Microsoft 365 account. It is the one you use for schoolwork.

  1. Go to office.com.
  2. Sign in with your school Microsoft account, not a personal one. If you are not sure which is which, your school account is the one with your school email address.
  3. Once you are signed in, you can open Word, PowerPoint, Excel, and OneDrive from that same page.

Everything you save while signed in to your school account is saved to your school OneDrive, where you and your teacher can both find it.

Your OneDrive folder for this course

Keep your schoolwork organized the way you would keep a binder organized. One folder per subject, one folder inside it per course.

For this course, your folder path is:

Optima > History > WorldHistory6

If those folders do not exist yet, make them:

  1. Open OneDrive from office.com.
  2. Click New, then Folder. Name the first one Optima.
  3. Open Optima, make a folder inside it named History.
  4. Open History, make a folder inside it named WorldHistory6.

If your teacher asks you to add the school year to the folder name, follow what your teacher tells you. Otherwise the name above is all you need.

Naming your files

Every file you turn in uses the same naming pattern. It looks like this:

LastName_FirstName_AssignmentName_CourseCode

The course code for this course is WH6.

So a student named Jane Smith, turning in the Comparative Essay for this course, would name her file:

Smith_Jane_ComparativeEssay_WH6_Final

A few rules that go with it:

  • Use underscores, not spaces.
  • The version you actually turn in always ends in _Final.
  • If you save a rough version first, end it in _Draft1 and keep it. Do not delete an earlier version or save over it. Keeping your drafts lets your teacher see how your thinking grew.

This naming rule may look fussy. It exists so that when a teacher opens a folder holding hundreds of files, yours is instantly findable, and so that your own work stays findable to you months later.

Which program to use

Match the tool to what you are making.

What you are making What to open
An essay, a report, or any writingWord
A slide presentationPowerPoint
A table of data or numbersExcel

For this course, the one assignment that asks for a file is the Comparative Essay at the end. That one is a Word document.

Turning your work in through Canvas

  1. Finish your document in Word and make sure it is saved in your WorldHistory6 folder.
  2. Open the assignment in Canvas and click Submit Assignment.
  3. Choose the OneDrive tab if you see one, then pick your file. If you do not see a OneDrive tab, choose File Upload and upload the document from your computer.
  4. Click Submit, then check that Canvas shows your file name back to you. If it does not, the file did not go through.

That last step matters. A submission you did not confirm is the most common way good work ends up ungraded.

One thing worth knowing about OneDrive

OneDrive saves as you type, and it keeps a history of your changes. If you delete a paragraph and want it back an hour later, you can open File, then Info, then Version History, and look at earlier versions of your own document.

This is a real habit worth building now: it means your work is never one mistake away from being lost.

If you joined this course partway through the year

Welcome. Do these four things and you will be caught up on the setup side:

  1. Check that you can sign in at office.com with your school account. If you cannot, message your teacher.
  2. Make your Optima > History > WorldHistory6 folder if it is not already there.
  3. Read the file naming rule above and bookmark this page.
  4. Ask your teacher whether any earlier assignment needs to be turned in.

Where to get help

Message your teacher through Canvas. If you want to practice a Word skill on your own, Microsoft keeps short beginner guides at support.microsoft.com.

assignments.title: 1.5 Critical Questions: The Jericho Excavation Account
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (the Jericho excavation account) and Lesson 1/Lesson 2.

Directions: Below are two key passages from the primary source reading and one question about each. After looking at each excerpt and question, return to the full excerpt and Lesson 2 to reason out your answer. These questions are not answered by a single sentence in the text; you must draw an inference from the evidence described.

  1. "Neither the wall nor the ditch could have been the work of a small or disorganized group; moving this much stone and cutting this much rock by hand would have required sustained, coordinated labor over a considerable stretch of time."

    What does the scale of this construction project suggest about how the people of Neolithic Jericho were organized, even though they had no writing, no metal tools, and (as far as we know) no formal government?

  2. "We cannot yet say with certainty why the people of this settlement built a wall, a ditch, and a tower on this scale."

    The passage goes on to offer three possible explanations: defense, flood control, and symbolic or ceremonial meaning. Using what you know from Lesson 1 about the trade-offs of early settled life, which explanation do you find most persuasive, and what evidence from the passage supports your choice?

assignments.title: 1.9 Primary Source Exercise: The Çatalhöyük Excavation Account
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (the Çatalhöyük excavation account).

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the evidence described in the passage and in what you have learned this week about early farming settlements. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. The passage notes that some houses show floors and platforms built directly on top of much older ones, "sometimes... many times over in the same house." Why might a family choose to keep rebuilding on the exact same spot for generations, instead of building a new house nearby? What does this pattern suggest about how people in Çatalhöyük thought about their homes and their ancestors?

  2. The report describes bucrania (plastered cattle skulls) mounted in many households but admits, "We do not know precisely what belief or practice these skulls represented." Historians often distinguish between evidence (what was physically found) and interpretation (what historians think it means). Identify one sentence in the passage that is pure evidence, and one sentence that is interpretation built on top of that evidence. What is the risk of treating an interpretation as if it were settled fact?

assignments.title: 1.11 VR Activity (Supplemental): Walk Neolithic Jericho's Wall and Tower
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students explore a reconstruction of Neolithic Jericho's stone wall, defensive ditch, and the circular stone tower, walking the interior stairway from base to summit. The environment presents the structure exactly as excavation established it: built before pottery, before metal tools, before writing.

What to do, in order:

  1. Walk along the base of the stone wall and look down into the rock-cut ditch running alongside it.
  2. Enter the tower and climb its internal stairway from the bottom to the top.
  3. At the top, look out over the surrounding settlement and countryside, and read the short optional notes along the way describing what was, and was not, found in the excavation layers.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences answering the lesson's open question: why might a community with no writing, no metal, and no pottery have built something this large? Submit your answer in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've reached the top of the tower and written your answer to the closing question.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Students sometimes expect the activity to hand them a settled answer for why the wall and tower were built. It does not, on purpose. If a student asks you directly, remind them the honest historical answer is still debated, and that noticing the disagreement is the point of the activity.

assignments.title: 1.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Assemble a Çatalhöyük House Interior
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students furnish and decorate a single Çatalhöyük household, choosing where to place a bucranium (plastered cattle skull) installation, painted wall scenes, sleeping platforms, and a roof-access ladder, then compare their choices with what excavation actually found.

What to do, in order:

  1. Look over the bare mudbrick room and the objects available to place inside it: a bucranium mount, a wall painting panel, sleeping platforms, storage areas, and a roof ladder.
  2. Place each object wherever in the room seems most sensible to you.
  3. Reveal the overlay showing where excavators actually found these features, and compare it to your own layout.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences describing one place where your layout matched what was actually found, and one place where it did not. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've placed every object, revealed the overlay, and written your comparison.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): The point of this activity is the compare-and-reveal moment, not getting the layout right on the first try. Encourage students to place objects by their own best guess before looking at the answer.

assignments.title: 2.5 Critical Questions: The Epic of Gilgamesh, Flood Tablet
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (the Gilgamesh Flood Tablet excerpt) and Lesson 2.

Directions: Below are two key passages from the assigned reading and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full primary source and the lesson to reason out your answer.

  1. "And Ea, the clever one, was sworn to secrecy with them, yet he repeated their plan to a reed fence... 'Man of Shuruppak, tear down your house, build a boat!'"

    Ea does not warn Utnapishtim directly; he speaks to a reed fence outside Utnapishtim's house. Why might the story include this odd detail about Ea technically keeping his oath of secrecy while still saving Utnapishtim's life? What does this suggest about how the gods in this story are bound by their own rules?

  2. "For six days and six nights the wind blew, the flood-storm flattened the land... I looked at the weather, and stillness had set in, and all mankind had turned back into clay."

    Utnapishtim describes the destruction of "all mankind" in stark terms. Based on Lesson 2's explanation of the Sumerian King List's own flood account, what might this shared memory of a catastrophic flood tell historians about actual events in ancient Mesopotamia, separate from the supernatural elements of the story?

assignments.title: 2.9 Primary Source Exercise: The Sumerian King List
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (the Sumerian King List excerpt).

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. The reign lengths recorded before the flood (in the tens of thousands of years) shrink dramatically to reigns of hundreds and then ordinary numbers of years after the flood. Why might Sumerian scribes have chosen to mark this shift so sharply at the flood, rather than having reign lengths decrease gradually over many generations?

  2. The list repeatedly uses the phrase "kingship descended from heaven" (used twice: once at the very beginning, and again after the flood). What idea about the nature of political authority is this phrase expressing, that is never directly explained in the text itself? What would it mean for a king's power to come from the gods rather than, for example, from military conquest or the consent of the people?

assignments.title: 2.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Explore a Ziggurat at Uruk
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students explore a reconstruction of Uruk's temple ziggurat, from the surrounding city streets and workshops at ground level, up the monumental stairway, to the temple platform at its summit.

What to do, in order:

  1. Begin at street level among the workshops, storage buildings, and canal-fed fields.
  2. Climb the ziggurat's stairway toward the temple platform at the top.
  3. Along the way, read the optional notes on how the temple worked as both a religious center and an economic hub, tracking grain and goods delivered from the surrounding farmland.

What to submit: In your own words, write two or three sentences explaining how the ziggurat's height and position connect to its economic role in Uruk. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've reached the temple platform and written your explanation.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Some students will focus only on the ziggurat's religious role and miss its economic one. Point them back to the notes about grain and goods if their written answer only mentions worship.

assignments.title: 2.13 VR Activity (Supplemental): Press a Stylus into Clay: A Cuneiform-Writing Simulation
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students use a virtual reed stylus to press wedge-shaped marks into a soft clay tablet, replicating a scribe's basic hand motions and building a short cuneiform sign or simple word under guided instruction.

What to do, in order:

  1. Practice the angled press-and-pull motion of the virtual reed stylus against the clay surface.
  2. Follow the guided instructions to form a small number of basic cuneiform signs.
  3. Compare your finished tablet to a photograph of an authentic excavated tablet bearing the same signs.

What to submit: Write one or two sentences describing what surprised you about how physically demanding this was. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've formed the assigned signs and compared your tablet to the real photograph.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): This is a fine motor skill activity, and some students will need a few tries before the wedge shapes come out cleanly. That struggle is intentional; it is part of what is being taught.

assignments.title: 3.5 Critical Questions: The Legend of Sargon
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (the Sargon Birth Legend) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two key passages from the assigned reading and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full primary source and the lesson to reason out your answer.

  1. "My mother was a high priestess; my father I never knew."

    Lesson 1 notes that the legend leaves Sargon's father entirely unnamed. Why might a text meant to celebrate a great king choose to begin with this kind of uncertain, humble parentage rather than a clear noble lineage?

  2. "While I was a gardener, the goddess Ishtar came to love me, and for many years I held kingship."

    The text moves directly from "gardener" to "kingship" with only the goddess's favor bridging the gap. What real, practical steps (not mentioned in this passage) would Sargon likely have needed to take between working as a gardener and actually ruling an empire? Why might the legend skip over them?

assignments.title: 3.9 Primary Source Exercise: The Curse of Akkad
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (the Curse of Akkad excerpt).

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. The poem lists agricultural disaster (no grain, no fish, no wine) immediately before describing the Gutian invasion. Using both the poem's own account and Lesson 2's explanation of drought evidence from soil and pollen records, construct your own explanation of how religious, political, and environmental causes might have combined to bring down the Akkadian Empire. Do not settle for naming only one cause.

  2. The poem describes the Gutians as a people "with human intelligence but canine instincts and monkeys' features," language clearly meant to dehumanize them. What does this tell you about how the Akkadian or Sumerian audience of this poem likely viewed outsiders who threatened their cities? Is this the only ancient or modern example you can think of where a civilization describes a rival people in less than fully human terms?

assignments.title: 3.11 VR Activity (Supplemental): Trace Sargon's Conquests on a Map of Mesopotamia
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students stand over a large-scale, walkable relief map of Mesopotamia and the surrounding region, watching Sargon's conquests unfold as a sequence of animated campaign routes, from Kish and Uruk outward to the Mediterranean coast and into Elam.

What to do, in order:

  1. Stand over the large relief map of Mesopotamia and the surrounding region.
  2. Trigger each campaign stage in order, watching Akkadian territory grow with each one.
  3. Pause at Kish, Uruk, and Akkad's approximate region to review the short notes on what each conquest added to the empire.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences on why holding this much territory together required the standardized administration described in Lesson 2. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've triggered every campaign stage and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Students sometimes rush through the campaign animation without reading the city notes. Encourage them to pause at each city rather than just watching the map fill in.

assignments.title: 3.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Examine an Akkadian Victory Stele Relief
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students examine a full-scale reconstruction of an Akkadian victory stele (a carved stone monument commemorating a king's military triumph), walking around it to study its carved registers up close.

What to do, in order:

  1. Circle the stele, studying its carved registers from more than one angle.
  2. Zoom into the details showing the king in triumph over defeated enemies.
  3. Read the short annotations explaining the visual conventions Akkadian artists used to signal royal power.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences identifying one specific visual convention this stele uses to show the king's power, and explain what it communicates. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've circled the stele, read the annotations, and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Some students will describe the scene generally without naming a specific convention (scale, weapons, captives). Push them toward naming one concrete visual detail.

assignments.title: 4.5 Critical Questions: The Code of Hammurabi (Selected Laws)
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (selected laws) and Lesson 2.

Directions: Below are two key passages from the assigned reading and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full primary source and the lesson to reason out your answer.

  1. "Law 196. If a man put out the eye of another man, his eye shall be put out. Law 198. If he put out the eye of a freed man (a mushkenum), or break the bone of a freed man, he shall pay one gold mina. Law 199. If he put out the eye of a man's slave, or break the bone of a man's slave, he shall pay one-half of the slave's value."

    Lesson 2 describes lex talionis as a limiting principle on revenge. Based on these three laws together, is lex talionis applied equally regardless of the victim's social class? Use specific details from all three laws to support your answer.

  2. "Law 218. If a physician makes a large incision with an operating knife and kills the patient... his hands shall be cut off."

    A physician who makes an honest but fatal mistake faces a severe, disfiguring punishment under this law. What tension might this create between encouraging skilled people to practice medicine at all and holding them accountable for patient safety? How might this law have shaped who was willing to become a physician in Babylon?

assignments.title: 4.9 Primary Source Exercise: The Prologue to the Code of Hammurabi
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (the Prologue).

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. The prologue claims Hammurabi was chosen by the gods Anu and Bel specifically "so that the strong should not harm the weak." Why might a king in Hammurabi's position, having just unified much of Mesopotamia through military conquest late in his reign, want to frame his rule this way rather than simply pointing to his armies as the source of his authority?

  2. Compare this prologue's claim, that Hammurabi's authority comes from the gods and is justified by protecting the weak from the strong, to the Sargon Birth Legend you read in Week 3, where royal authority came from an improbable rise and the favor of the goddess Ishtar. What does each text suggest a Mesopotamian audience expected a legitimate king to demonstrate?

assignments.title: 4.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Inspect the Hammurabi Stele Relief
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students examine a full-scale reconstruction of Hammurabi's law stele, including the carved relief at its top showing Hammurabi receiving his authority from the sun-god Shamash, and the columns of cuneiform law text carved below.

What to do, in order:

  1. Circle the stele to study the relief scene of Hammurabi receiving authority from Shamash.
  2. Trace down the carved columns of law text to see, at true scale, how much law is inscribed on the monument.
  3. Compare the stele's public, standing placement to the private clay tablets used for everyday records in Weeks 2 and 3.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences on why a public, monumental law code works differently than a private administrative record. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've inspected the relief, traced the text columns, and written your comparison.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): The comparison to Weeks 2 and 3's clay tablets is the heart of this activity. If a student's answer only describes the relief scene, ask them to bring in that comparison directly.

assignments.title: 4.13 VR Activity (Supplemental): A Courtroom Simulation, Judge a Case Under the Code
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students take the role of a judge in an Old Babylonian courtroom, hearing a short dispute (for example, a builder whose house has collapsed, or a tavern-keeper accused of shortchanging a customer) and applying the relevant law from this week's Primary Source 1 to reach a verdict.

What to do, in order:

  1. Listen to both sides of the staged dispute.
  2. Locate the applicable law among the excerpted laws from this week's primary source.
  3. Render your verdict, then compare it and your reasoning to the Code's actual specified penalty.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences on whether your verdict matched the Code's, and if not, what you missed. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've heard the dispute, located the law, and written your comparison.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Students will sometimes render a fair-sounding verdict that does not match the actual law. That mismatch is a useful discussion point, not a failure; ask what in the law's wording they missed.

assignments.title: 5.5 Critical Questions: The Narmer Palette
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (the Narmer Palette) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two excerpts describing specific registers of the Narmer Palette and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 description and to Lesson 1 to reason out your answer.

  1. "A falcon, identified with the god Horus, perched on a clump of papyrus plants... and holding a rope tied through the nose of a human head that emerges from the same papyrus clump, another image widely read as a personification of conquered Lower Egyptian territory."

    Papyrus was strongly associated with Lower Egypt. Using Lesson 1's account of Narmer's unification, explain what this image is likely trying to communicate about the relationship between the king, the god Horus, and the northern land being subdued.

  2. "Some historians read the Palette as a documentary record of one specific, historical military campaign that achieved Egypt's unification. Others argue it is closer to a formal, symbolic statement of the king's role as unifier and conqueror... compressed here into a single ceremonial image."

    Which of these two readings do you find more persuasive, and why? Use at least one specific detail from the Palette's registers to support your reasoning, rather than a general impression.

assignments.title: 5.9 Primary Source Exercise: The Instructions of Ptahhotep
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (the Instructions of Ptahhotep) and Lesson 2.

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. Suppose the Instructions of Ptahhotep had never survived, and every Old Kingdom text we possessed today was a royal monument like the Narmer Palette or an inscription praising a pharaoh's building projects. How would our whole picture of what Old Kingdom Egyptians valued be different, or incomplete, without a text like this one?

  2. Compare Ptahhotep's advice on how a leader should listen to a petitioner ("do not rebuff him before he has unburdened himself... a man who has suffered wrong wants his heart to be eased even more than he wants his case to succeed") to Hammurabi's Code from Week 4, which spelled out exact penalties for specific wrongs. Which approach, precise written law or a leader's personal patience and character, does more to make ordinary people feel they have received justice? Can a society need both at once?

assignments.title: 5.11 VR Activity (Supplemental): Walk the Causeway to the Great Pyramid Construction Site
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students walk a reconstructed causeway and construction yard at Giza during the Great Pyramid's building, observing ramps, work gangs, sledges hauling stone blocks, and the workers' village with its bakeries and cattle pens described in Lesson 2.

What to do, in order:

  1. Follow a stone block's path from the quarry, up a ramp, into position on the rising pyramid.
  2. Visit the workers' village to see its bakeries, breweries, and housing.
  3. Compare this organized, provisioned worksite to the popular image of slave-driven mass labor.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences on what evidence in the workers' village argues against the mass-slavery image of pyramid building. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've followed the block's path, visited the village, and written your comparison.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Many students arrive with the slave-labor image from popular culture. This activity is built to complicate that, not simply announce it is wrong. Let students work out the argument themselves.

assignments.title: 5.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Explore Old Kingdom Tomb Art
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students explore a reconstructed Old Kingdom mastaba tomb chamber, examining painted and carved scenes of daily life, farming, fishing, offering rituals, and inscriptions naming the tomb's owner and their titles.

What to do, in order:

  1. Move through the tomb's chapel and offering chamber.
  2. Identify scenes of everyday Old Kingdom life carved into the walls: farming, fishing, offerings.
  3. Compare these domestic scenes to the divine, cosmic imagery of the Narmer Palette studied earlier this week.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences comparing one everyday tomb scene to the Narmer Palette's cosmic imagery. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've toured the tomb chamber and written your comparison.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Students may need a reminder of what the Narmer Palette showed before they can make this comparison. Have Lesson 1 or its primary source handy to reference.

assignments.title: 6.5 Critical Questions: Hatshepsut's Punt Expedition Inscriptions
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (the Punt expedition inscriptions) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two excerpts from Hatshepsut's Punt inscriptions and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 text and to Lesson 1 to reason out your answer.

  1. "How is it that you have come here, to this land which the people of Egypt do not know? Have you come down from the roads of heaven, or have you sailed upon the waters of the sea of God's Land?"

    This speech is placed in the mouth of Parehu, the chief of Punt, describing the Egyptians as if their arrival were almost supernatural. Whose interests does this framing actually serve, the people of Punt, or Hatshepsut's own government back in Egypt? Explain your reasoning.

  2. "Never was brought the like of this for any king who has ruled since the beginning of the world."

    This is a bold claim to be the greatest such expedition in all of Egyptian history. Using Lesson 1's account of Hatshepsut's unusual and contested path to the throne, explain why a monumental claim like this one might have mattered especially to her, more than it might have mattered to a pharaoh whose right to rule was never in question.

assignments.title: 6.9 Primary Source Exercise: The Annals of Thutmose III (The Battle of Megiddo)
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (the Annals of Thutmose III) and Lesson 2.

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. The Annals record that Thutmose III's officers argued for one of the two safer roads to Megiddo. Suppose Thutmose III had listened to them instead of insisting on the narrow pass. Based on what the text says actually happened once the Egyptian army emerged from the pass unopposed, how might the whole campaign have unfolded differently on a safer road?

  2. Compare Thutmose III's own explanation for choosing the narrow pass ("my majesty will proceed upon this narrow road... let whoever wishes come in the following of my majesty") to Hatshepsut's Punt inscription from earlier this week, where the credit for the voyage is given to the will of the god Amun. Which ruler's text gives more credit to personal judgment, and which gives more credit to the gods? Does this difference match the different paths to greatness Lesson 1 and Lesson 2 describe for each ruler?

assignments.title: 6.10 VR Activity: Hatshepsut and Thutmose III: Two Paths to Greatness
assignments.html:
This week's required VR activity. A split exploration comparing two reconstructed environments: the Punt reliefs at Hatshepsut's mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, and the terrain of the Megiddo campaign, including the narrow Aruna pass and the plain before the city.

What you will do: In the first half, examine the Deir el-Bahari Punt reliefs up close, identifying the goods loaded onto Hatshepsut's ships and the diplomatic framing of the encounter with Punt's chief. In the second half, stand at the mouth of the Aruna pass, look down its narrow, single-file length, and then view the open plain before Megiddo where Thutmose III's gamble paid off.

Time: About 25 to 30 minutes.

What to do, in order:

  1. Examine the Deir el-Bahari Punt reliefs up close, identifying the goods loaded onto Hatshepsut's ships.
  2. Note the diplomatic framing of the encounter with Punt's chief shown in the reliefs.
  3. Stand at the mouth of the Aruna pass and look down its narrow, single-file length.
  4. View the open plain before Megiddo where Thutmose III's gamble paid off.
  5. Write your judgment: which ruler's approach, trade and diplomacy or a bold personal military gamble, better solved Egypt's first-order problems of security and prosperity? Use specific details from both environments.

What to submit: Write a response, grounded in specific details from both environments, judging which ruler's approach, trade and diplomacy or a bold personal military gamble, better solved Egypt's first-order problems of security and prosperity. Cite at least one specific detail from each environment. Engage honestly with the trade-offs of each approach rather than dismissing either ruler's path as simply inferior. Submit in Canvas.

You'll know you're done when: You've examined both environments and submitted a judgment citing specific details from each.

assignments.title: 6.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): A Focused Walkthrough of the Punt Expedition
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students walk the deck of a reconstructed Egyptian trading ship on the Red Sea voyage to Punt, then step ashore to observe the loading of incense trees, exotic animals, and goods described in Lesson 1 and Primary Source 1.

What to do, in order:

  1. Explore the ship's cargo hold before it is loaded, noting the empty space.
  2. Explore the same hold after loading, comparing the space each good (incense trees, ebony, ivory, animals) requires.
  3. Examine the shoreline encounter with Punt's own people and dwellings.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences on what the cargo comparison shows about the logistics of a major ancient trading expedition. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've compared both cargo states and examined the shoreline scene.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Some students will focus only on the exotic goods and miss the logistics point, how much space and planning this required. Steer them toward the before-and-after comparison specifically.

assignments.title: 7.5 Critical Questions: Marshall's Mohenjo-daro Excavation Report (1924)
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (Marshall's excavation report) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two excerpts from Marshall's excavation report and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 text and to Lesson 1 to reason out your answer.

  1. "We have searched for a structure we might confidently call a palace, or a great temple built to rival those of Sumer or Egypt, and to date we have found neither. This is, I confess, a puzzle I cannot yet resolve."

    Marshall admits uncertainty directly, rather than guessing confidently. Why is this kind of honest admission valuable in a scientific excavation report, even though it leaves the reader without a clear answer? What would be lost if Marshall had simply invented a confident explanation instead?

  2. "Nearly every house we have excavated connects to a covered drain running beneath the street... Such attention to sanitation, at this date, we have not observed in any other ancient city yet excavated."

    Using Lesson 1's account of Indus urban planning, explain what building citywide drainage and standardized bricks across a huge territory would have required in terms of coordinated effort, even without any known king to have ordered it. Does the existence of this infrastructure count as evidence for or against the idea that Indus society had some form of centralized authority?

assignments.title: 7.9 Primary Source Exercise: Shang Oracle Bone Inscriptions
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (the oracle bone inscriptions) and Lesson 2.

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. The note on Lady Hao's childbirth inscription observes that a daughter's birth was recorded as "not good." Without using the word directly, what does this reveal about a value system at work in Shang court culture regarding heirs and gender, and how does it sit alongside the same royal family entrusting a woman, Fu Hao, with military command?

  2. Compare the oracle bone entry ordering "Lady Fu Hao to lead the troops in an attack against the Tu Fang" to Hatshepsut's Punt inscriptions from Week 6, another primary source describing a woman exercising major state authority in the ancient world. What is similar, and what is different, about how each text presents a woman's authority as legitimate?

assignments.title: 7.10 VR Activity: Cities Without Kings: Mohenjo-daro and Anyang Compared
assignments.html:
This week's required VR activity. A side-by-side exploration of reconstructed Mohenjo-daro and Anyang, letting you walk both cities and compare what kind of authority, or absence of it, shaped each one.

What you will do: In Mohenjo-daro, walk the gridded streets, examine the covered drains and private wells, and search, deliberately in vain, for any palace or grand temple. In Anyang, walk among Shang royal structures and view a reconstruction of Fu Hao's tomb, with its bronzes and inscriptions naming real historical people.

Time: About 20 to 25 minutes.

What to do, in order:

  1. Walk the gridded streets of Mohenjo-daro.
  2. Examine the covered drains and private wells.
  3. Search deliberately for any palace or grand temple in Mohenjo-daro. You will not find one.
  4. Walk among Shang royal structures in Anyang.
  5. View the reconstruction of Fu Hao's tomb, including its bronzes and inscriptions naming real historical people.
  6. Write your comparison: what physical, visible evidence of authority is present at Anyang that is entirely missing at Mohenjo-daro? What does that difference, or its absence, actually prove versus merely suggest?

What to submit: Write a response comparing the physical, visible evidence of authority in each city: what is present at Anyang that is entirely missing at Mohenjo-daro, and what does that difference, or its absence, actually prove versus merely suggest? Distinguish clearly between what the evidence proves and what it merely leaves open, rather than treating Mohenjo-daro's missing palace as proof of any single, confident theory about Indus government. Submit in Canvas.

You'll know you're done when: You've explored both cities and submitted a comparison naming specific evidence from each.

assignments.title: 7.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Crack an Oracle Bone
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. A divination simulator letting students act as a Shang diviner, applying a heated point to a virtual oracle bone, observing the resulting crack pattern, and recording a question and outcome in oracle bone script alongside it.

What to do, in order:

  1. Choose a question in the style of this week's Primary Source 2, about weather, health, or a military campaign.
  2. Apply heat to the virtual oracle bone and observe where it cracks.
  3. Record the question and a plausible interpreted outcome, mirroring the format seen in the primary source.

What to submit: Write one or two sentences on how recording your question and outcome felt similar to or different from the real oracle bone inscription. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've cracked the bone and recorded your question and outcome.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Students may want the crack pattern to have one single correct reading. Remind them that interpretation was part of the diviner's role in real Shang practice, not a fixed answer key.

assignments.title: 8.5 Critical Questions: The Egyptian-Hittite Peace Treaty
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (the Egyptian-Hittite Peace Treaty) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two excerpts from the treaty and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 text and to Lesson 1 to reason out your answer.

  1. "The great chief of Hatti shall never again enter the land of Egypt, to take anything from it. And Ramesses, the great ruler of Egypt, shall never again enter the land of Hatti, to take anything from it."

    This clause binds both sides to identical, mirrored promises rather than favoring one side over the other. Using Lesson 1's account of the Battle of Kadesh's inconclusive outcome, explain why a treaty written this way, as an agreement between equals, might have been the only kind of peace both empires were actually willing to accept.

  2. "If any other enemy comes against the lands of the great ruler of Egypt, and he sends word to the great chief of Hatti saying, 'Come with me as reinforcement against him,' the great chief of Hatti shall come."

    This clause commits each empire to defend the other against a third party, not merely to leave each other alone. Why might two former enemies choose to bind themselves this closely together, rather than settling for a simpler promise to stop fighting each other?

assignments.title: 8.9 Primary Source Exercise: Homer's Iliad, the Catalogue of Ships
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (the Catalogue of Ships) and Lesson 2.

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. Agamemnon leads a hundred ships, the largest contingent by far, and the text calls him "the mightiest of all the chiefs, for he brought by far the greatest army of any." Using Lesson 2's account of the Mycenaean palace economy and its wanax-centered hierarchy, why might the size of a king's fleet, rather than some other measure entirely, have served ancient audiences as the clearest sign of a Mycenaean ruler's real power and status?

  2. Compare Nestor's introduction, "wisest counselor among the Greeks... age had made him no less valuable in council than in war," to Ptahhotep's advice from Week 5 that good judgment "can never be reached" by anyone alone and that wisdom "may be found even among servant girls grinding grain." What does each text suggest about where a society expects wisdom to come from, and whether age or rank is the only source of it?

assignments.title: 8.10 VR Activity: Forge Hittite Iron at Hattusa
assignments.html:
This week's required VR activity. Visit a reconstructed Hittite smithy within the fortified city of Hattusa, and work through the stages of early ironworking: smelting ore into a bloom, hammering out slag, and shaping a finished iron blade.

What you will do: Operate a simulated smelting furnace, work the resulting iron bloom under a hammer, and produce a finished object. A guided narration contrasts this scene with the popular "Hittite iron monopoly, guarded as a state secret" story, presenting the more gradual, widespread picture of early ironworking that current scholarship supports.

Time: About 20 minutes.

What to do, in order:

  1. Enter the reconstructed Hittite smithy within the fortified city of Hattusa.
  2. Operate the simulated smelting furnace to turn ore into a bloom.
  3. Work the resulting iron bloom under a hammer to drive out slag.
  4. Shape the hammered bloom into a finished iron blade.
  5. Listen to the guided narration contrasting this scene with the popular "Hittite iron monopoly, guarded as a state secret" story.
  6. Write a short reflection distinguishing the older popular myth from the more accurate, gradual-adoption picture Lesson 1 describes.

What to submit: Write a short reflection describing what early ironworking actually required, and explicitly correct the outdated "secret monopoly" version of the Hittite iron story with the more accurate, gradual-adoption picture from Lesson 1. Do not repeat the "secret monopoly" framing uncritically. Submit in Canvas.

You'll know you're done when: You've completed all three smithing stages and submitted a reflection correcting the "secret monopoly" myth.

assignments.title: 8.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Tour the Unwalled Minoan Palace at Knossos
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students walk the sprawling palace complex at Knossos, exploring its storage magazines, workshops, plumbing, and open, unwalled approach from the surrounding countryside.

What to do, in order:

  1. Move through the palace's corridors and courtyards.
  2. Examine its terracotta plumbing and light-wells.
  3. Walk the palace's open perimeter, noting the complete absence of any defensive wall, and consider the competing explanations Lesson 2 raises for why.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences on which explanation for the missing wall you find most convincing, and why. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've toured the palace, the plumbing, and the perimeter, and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): This is another genuinely unresolved historical question. If a student wants the real answer, remind them that historians disagree and that reasoning through the possibilities is the actual assignment.

assignments.title: 9.5 Critical Questions: Ramesses III's Medinet Habu Inscription
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (the Medinet Habu inscription) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two excerpts from the Medinet Habu inscription and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 text and to Lesson 1 to reason out your answer.

  1. "No land could stand before their arms, from Hatti, Kode, Carchemish, Arzawa, and Cyprus onward, all being cut off at one time."

    This line names several specific lands, including Hatti, as already fallen before the Sea Peoples reach Egypt. Using Lesson 1's account of the wider Bronze Age Collapse, why might Ramesses III have wanted to list these other fallen powers by name in his own inscription, rather than describing Egypt's own struggle in isolation?

  2. "I have made the lands turn back from even mentioning Egypt, for when they say the name of my majesty in their land, it burns their bodies."

    This is a royal inscription meant to celebrate the pharaoh's total victory. Given that Lesson 1 describes Egypt's power as never fully recovering afterward, how should a historian weigh a triumphant royal claim like this one against what actually happened to Egypt in the following decades?

assignments.title: 9.9 Primary Source Exercise: Pylos's "Rower Tablets"
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (the rower and o-ka tablets) and Lesson 2.

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. Suppose these tablets had survived unburned, stored safely in an archive somewhere, with no accompanying evidence that Pylos itself was ever destroyed. Would historians today read these same watch-post and rowing-muster lists as evidence of a crisis at all, or simply as routine palace bookkeeping? What does this suggest about how much a document's meaning depends on what we already know happened afterward?

  2. Compare the terse, numbers-only style of these Pylos tablets ("Ro-o-wa: two men. Timito-akee: ten men.") to Ramesses III's confident, elaborate inscription from earlier this week. What does the difference in tone and form between these two texts suggest about the difference between a document meant only for a palace's own internal use and one meant to be read, and to impress, for centuries afterward?

assignments.title: 9.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Man Pylos's Coastal Watch in Its Final Days
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students take up a post at one of the coastal watch stations described in the o-ka tablets, scanning the sea for approaching ships during Pylos's final, uneasy season before its destruction.

What to do, in order:

  1. Take up your post at the reconstructed coastal watch station.
  2. Observe the surrounding landscape and sea, watching for approaching ships.
  3. Review the simplified muster list assigning men to that post, and respond to the closing prompt about what the watchers themselves might or might not have known.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences, without inventing false certainty, on what you think the watchers knew or suspected about the danger they were watching for. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've stood watch, reviewed the muster list, and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): The point here is restraint, not drama. If a student's answer claims the watchers definitely knew doom was coming, ask what evidence in the tablets actually supports that versus what they are imagining.

assignments.title: 9.13 VR Activity (Supplemental): Compare Ruins: Which Bronze Age Capitals Burned, and Which Endured?
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. A comparative walkthrough of several Bronze Age capitals this course has studied, Hattusa, Mycenae, Memphis, and Babylon, shown in their post-collapse states, some destroyed and abandoned, others damaged but still inhabited and functioning.

What to do, in order:

  1. Visit each of the four capitals (Hattusa, Mycenae, Memphis, Babylon) in its condition shortly after the collapse period.
  2. At each site, note whether it shows destruction and abandonment, or continued, diminished activity.
  3. Match each site to the outcome Lesson 2 describes for it.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences identifying which site surprised you most, and why. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've visited all four sites and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Students sometimes assume every Bronze Age capital was destroyed. Point out at the start that the activity is built specifically to show that this was not true everywhere.

assignments.title: 10.5 Critical Questions: The Great Triumphal Stele of Piye
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (Piye's Great Triumphal Stele) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two excerpts from Piye's stele and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 text and to Lesson 1 to reason out your answer.

  1. "I swear, as Re loves me, and as my nostrils are rejuvenated with life, it is more grievous in my heart that my horses have suffered hunger, than any evil deed that thou hast done, in the prosecution of thy desire."

    Piye directs this remark at a defeated human rival, over the treatment of animals rather than any political offense. Using Lesson 1's discussion, what does this detail suggest about how Piye's stele wants him to be remembered, compared to a ruler who simply boasts of conquest?

  2. "They entered not into the king's house, because they were unclean and eaters of fish; which is an abomination for the palace."

    Some defeated princes send tribute but never enter Piye's presence at all, since Egyptian custom viewed fish-eating peoples of the Delta marshes as ritually unclean. What does this detail suggest about the limits of Piye's authority over the Delta princes, even after his victory?

assignments.title: 10.9 Primary Source Exercise: Herodotus, Histories Book II
assignments.html:
These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. Compare Herodotus's own reasoned explanation for the Nile's summer flooding ("the Sun passing in his course by the upper parts of Libya... draws to himself the water, and having drawn it he drives it away to the upper parts") to his account of the phoenix, which he introduces by admitting he "did not myself see except in painting." What is the difference between a writer offering his own explanation for something he cannot observe directly, and a writer passing along a story he was simply told? Why might both appear in the same book?

  2. Herodotus writes that he traveled to a region in Arabia specifically "to inquire about the winged serpents," and reports that he "saw bones of serpents and spines in quantity so great that it is impossible to make report of the number." Yet modern historians remain skeptical that winged serpents ever existed. What does this example suggest about the difference between a writer honestly reporting what he believes he witnessed and that same account actually being reliable evidence?

assignments.title: 10.11 VR Activity (Supplemental): Read Piye's Stele: A King Who Fights for the Gods, Not Glory
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students stand before a reconstructed version of Piye's Great Triumphal Stele at Napata, examining its carved scenes and inscribed text panel by panel as a guided narration walks through the campaign it records.

What to do, in order:

  1. Move along the stele's carved surface, inspecting the scenes of Piye's army advancing.
  2. Inspect the scene of the Delta princes' submission and the inspection of Namlot's stables.
  3. Identify which moment on the stele most shapes how Piye wanted to be remembered, and why.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences naming the moment you chose and explaining your reasoning. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've inspected the stele's panels and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Students may default to the most dramatic-looking scene without connecting it to Piye's own self-presentation. Ask what the scene says about Piye specifically, not just what it depicts.

assignments.title: 10.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Separate Herodotus's Eyewitness Account from His Tall Tales
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students walk through a reconstructed Egyptian temple and embalming workshop alongside a narrating figure representing Herodotus, encountering a mix of plausible eyewitness observations and openly doubted traveler's tales along the way.

What to do, in order:

  1. Visit the mummification workshop, the riverside Nile-flood observation point, and the temple courtyard where the phoenix story is told.
  2. At each stop, sort the account into eyewitness reporting or tall tale, using Herodotus's own words as evidence.
  3. Check your answers against the built-in key.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences on which sorting decision was hardest to make, and why. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've sorted all three stops and checked your answers.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): The phoenix story is designed to be the trickiest sort, since Herodotus reports it while also voicing his own doubt. Expect questions about that one specifically.

assignments.title: 11.5 Critical Questions: Ashurnasirpal II's Annals
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (Ashurnasirpal II's Annals) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two excerpts from Ashurnasirpal II's inscriptions and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 text and to Lesson 1 to reason out your answer.

  1. "I built a pillar over against his city gate, and I flayed all the chief men who had revolted, and I covered the pillar with their skins."

    Why would Ashurnasirpal have this act publicly displayed and carved into a permanent record, rather than carrying it out quietly?

  2. "When I inaugurated the palace at Calah I treated for ten days with food and drink 47,074 persons."

    Using Lesson 1's framing, how does this feast serve a similar political purpose to the violence described elsewhere in the same set of inscriptions, even though the methods are completely different?

assignments.title: 11.9 Primary Source Exercise: The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III
assignments.html:
These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. The epigraph lists what Shalmaneser III "received" from Jehu as tribute: "silver, gold, a golden saplu-bowl, a golden vase with a pointed bottom, golden tumblers, golden buckets, tin, a staff for a king, and spear-shafts." Given Lesson 1's description of Assyria's military machine, why might a smaller kingdom's ruler send prized goods, including a symbolic royal staff, rather than face continued war?

  2. The epigraph identifies Jehu as "son of Omri," even though Jehu had violently ended Omri's own dynasty to take the Israelite throne himself. What does this naming choice suggest about how Assyrian scribes recorded defeated kingdoms, and what caution should a historian keep in mind when reading a name like this at face value?

assignments.title: 11.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Examine Ashurnasirpal's Palace Reliefs at Nimrud
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students walk through a reconstructed hall of Ashurnasirpal II's palace at Nimrud, examining the large carved stone reliefs that lined its walls, depicting royal hunts, military campaigns, and ceremonial scenes.

What to do, in order:

  1. Move along the palace corridor, inspecting the relief panels up close.
  2. Compare the propaganda purpose of these images to the written annals described in Lesson 1.
  3. Identify what a visitor to this palace, whether ambassador, vassal, or rebel in chains, was meant to feel while walking through it.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences on what a visitor was meant to feel, and which specific relief detail supports your answer. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've walked the corridor and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Students sometimes describe the reliefs only as art. Steer them toward the propaganda function, since that is the point Lesson 1 makes about the written annals too.

assignments.title: 11.13 VR Activity (Supplemental): Identify Jehu on the Black Obelisk
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students examine a full-scale reconstruction of the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, rotating around its four sides to locate the specific register depicting Jehu's submission among the other tribute scenes.

What to do, in order:

  1. Circle the obelisk, comparing its several carved registers.
  2. Identify the panel matching this week's Primary Source 2 inscription.
  3. Inspect the tribute goods carried by the attendants behind Jehu.

What to submit: Write one or two sentences describing what the tribute scene shows about Jehu's position relative to Shalmaneser III. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've found Jehu's register and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Students sometimes have trouble locating the correct register among the obelisk's four sides. Let them know it is fine to circle the monument more than once.

assignments.title: 12.5 Critical Questions: Ashurbanipal's Library Tablets
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (Ashurbanipal's Library Tablets) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two excerpts from Ashurbanipal's inscriptions and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 text and to Lesson 1 to reason out your answer.

  1. "I, Ashurbanipal, within the palace, understood the wisdom of Nabu... I learned the craft of the sage Adapa, the secret, hidden lore, all of the scribal arts."

    Lesson 1 notes that reading and writing were normally left entirely to trained scribes, not kings. Why might Ashurbanipal have wanted this specific detail about his own education recorded and preserved?

  2. "I have transcribed upon tablets the noble products of the work of the scribe which none of the kings who have gone before me had learned... Whosoever shall carry off this tablet, or shall inscribe his name on it, side by side with mine own, may Ashur and Belit overthrow him in wrath and anger, and may they destroy his name and posterity in the land."

    This colophon boasts that no earlier king had gathered such a collection, in the very same breath that it threatens a curse against anyone who damages or steals a tablet from it. What does the existence of both the boast and the curse together suggest about how valuable Ashurbanipal considered the library's contents?

assignments.title: 12.9 Primary Source Exercise: The Babylonian Chronicle (on the Fall of Nineveh)
assignments.html:
These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. Lesson 2 describes a succession crisis following Ashurbanipal's death as a major factor in Assyria's collapse. Gadd's chronicle entries move directly from "junction effected between Babylonians, Medes, and Scythians. March against Nineveh" to the siege and "capture of Nineveh," with no mention of any succession crisis at all. What does this gap suggest about the difference between what a terse chronicle chooses to record and the fuller set of causes a historian must piece together from multiple sources?

  2. The chronicle notes the captured city was "turned into a mound and a ruin," then records only the "departure of Kyaxares" and further booty for Nabopolassar, with no comment on what became of Assyria as a state. Compare this flat, businesslike tone to Ashurnasirpal's own annals from Week 11 or Ramesses III's inscription from Week 9. What does the difference in tone suggest about who each document was written for, and why?

assignments.title: 12.10 VR Activity: Ashurbanipal's Library: What Survived the Fire That Destroyed Nineveh?
assignments.html:
This week's required VR activity. Explore a reconstructed version of Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh, first browsing its shelves of clay tablets in their original state, then experiencing a simulated version of the fire that destroyed the palace in 612 BC, and finally examining which tablets an archaeologist might recover afterward.

What you will do: Browse labeled tablets across several subject areas (literature, astronomy, medicine, administration), observe the simulated fire moving through the palace, and then, in a following scene, sort recovered fragments into the categories of "hardened and legible," "damaged but partially readable," and "lost," using what Lesson 1 explains about how fire affects unbaked clay.

Time: About 25 minutes.

What to do, in order:

  1. Browse labeled tablets across several subject areas (literature, astronomy, medicine, administration) in Ashurbanipal's library.
  2. Observe the simulated fire moving through the palace in 612 BC.
  3. In the following scene, sort recovered fragments into "hardened and legible," "damaged but partially readable," and "lost," using what Lesson 1 explains about how fire affects unbaked clay.
  4. Write a closing reflection explaining, in your own words, the irony connecting the fire's destruction to the tablets' survival.

What to submit: Write a closing reflection that correctly explains how unbaked clay tablets were hardened, not destroyed, by the palace fire, and connects this directly to why so much of the library survived for modern recovery, per Lesson 1. Submit in Canvas.

You'll know you're done when: You've sorted the recovered fragments and submitted a reflection explaining the fire's role in preserving the tablets.

assignments.title: 12.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Walk Nineveh's Walls in the Empire's Final Days
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students walk along Nineveh's massive defensive walls during the siege described in this week's Babylonian Chronicle excerpt, observing the scale of the city's fortifications and the besieging Babylonian-Median forces beyond them.

What to do, in order:

  1. Move along the wall's ramparts.
  2. Observe the surrounding siege works and the besieging Babylonian-Median forces beyond the walls.
  3. Review the simplified timeline of the three-month siege drawn from the Babylonian Chronicle, and consider how a defender on these walls, unaware of the empire's fate, might have judged the city's chances.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences answering that question from the defender's point of view. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've walked the ramparts, reviewed the timeline, and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Students should reason from what a defender could actually have seen and known at the time, not from hindsight about Nineveh's fall. Redirect answers that lean only on the idea that they must have known it was hopeless.

assignments.title: 13.5 Critical Questions: The Babylonian Chronicles (on the Siege of Jerusalem)
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (the Babylonian Chronicle on the 597 BC capture of Jerusalem) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two key passages from the chronicle's entry for this event and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 text and to Lesson 1 to reason out your answer.

  1. "...marched to the Hatti-land, and encamped against the city of Judah, and on the second day of the month of Adar he captured the city and seized its king."

    The chronicle records the capture of Jerusalem and its king in this same flat, businesslike tone it uses for any other campaign. Using Lesson 2's account of what happened next to the captured king Jehoiachin, what does this terse phrase, "seized its king," turn out to stand for once you know the fuller story?

  2. "He appointed there a king of his own choice, and, having received its heavy tribute, sent (them) to Babylon."

    Rather than destroying Jerusalem outright in 597 BC, the chronicle states that Nebuchadnezzar appointed a new king of his own choice after capturing the city and receiving its tribute. Using Week 11's vocabulary, what kind of relationship does this describe between Judah and Babylon at this point?

assignments.title: 13.9 Primary Source Exercise: Nebuchadnezzar II's Building Inscriptions
assignments.html:
These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. Nebuchadnezzar's inscription claims that "in order to complete Etemenanki, I mobilized all countries everywhere." This great building project, and the Ishtar Gate alongside it, went up during the very same years his armies were destroying Jerusalem and deporting its people, described in this week's first Primary Source. What might explain a king pursuing both enormous building projects and destructive military campaigns during the same reign, rather than treating these as unrelated activities?

  2. Suppose Nebuchadnezzar's building inscriptions, describing gates that gave "splendor for the wonder of all people" and a ziggurat raised as "the wonder of the people of the world," were the only surviving evidence historians had about his reign, with no chronicle and no memory of Judah's exile at all. What aspect of his reign would be completely missing from that picture, and what does this suggest about the danger of judging a ruler's full impact from his own self-glorifying monuments alone?

assignments.title: 13.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Walk Through a Reconstruction of the Ishtar Gate
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students walk through a reconstructed Ishtar Gate and the ceremonial processional way leading to it, examining the glazed blue brickwork and its rows of sculpted bulls and dragons up close.

What to do, in order:

  1. Approach the gate from the processional way.
  2. Inspect individual glazed brick panels and their animal imagery up close.
  3. Compare the gate's scale and color to other monumental structures this course has studied (Egyptian temples, Assyrian palaces), and consider the impression it was designed to leave on a first-time visitor.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences describing that impression, in your own words. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've walked the processional way, inspected the brickwork, and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Encourage students to actually make the comparison to earlier weeks' monuments rather than describing the gate in isolation; that comparison is what the activity is testing.

assignments.title: 13.13 VR Activity (Supplemental): Trace the Road of Exile, Jerusalem to Babylon
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students trace the overland route deportees would have traveled from Jerusalem to Babylon following the city's fall, observing the changing landscape and distance involved.

What to do, in order:

  1. Follow the overland route on the scaled terrain map, starting from Jerusalem.
  2. Pause at several waypoints to review short notes on what is and is not known about the deportees' experience.
  3. Arrive at Babylon and compare its scale and grandeur to Jerusalem's.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences on how the physical distance of this route shaped the challenge of maintaining identity in exile. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've followed the route to Babylon and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Some students will want more certainty about the deportees' day-to-day experience than the record actually supports. The waypoint notes are written to be honest about that gap; reinforce it if asked.

assignments.title: 14.5 Critical Questions: Herodotus on Deioces and the Founding of Media
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (Herodotus on Deioces) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two excerpts from Herodotus's account of Deioces and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 text and to Lesson 1 to reason out your answer.

  1. "As the Medes at that time dwelt in scattered villages without any central authority, and lawlessness in consequence prevailed throughout the land, Deioces... applied himself with greater zeal and earnestness than ever before to the practice of justice among his fellows."

    What does this detail suggest about how Deioces's authority is said to have begun, compared to conquerors like Sargon or Piye this course has studied in earlier weeks?

  2. "He allowed no one to have direct access to the person of the king, but made all communication pass through the hands of messengers, and forbade the king to be seen by his subjects. He also made it an offence for any one whatsoever to laugh or spit in the royal presence."

    What does this detail suggest Deioces understood about the difference between being trusted as a fair neighbor and being obeyed as a king?

assignments.title: 14.9 Primary Source Exercise: Herodotus's Account of the Battle of the Eclipse
assignments.html:
These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. The text describes five years of indecisive war in which "the Medes often discomfited the Lydians and the Lydians often discomfited the Medes," before the eclipse turned day to night in the sixth year. Suppose no eclipse had occurred that year. Based on this description of years of back-and-forth fighting, do you think the two sides would eventually have made peace anyway, or fought on much longer? Explain your reasoning.

  2. Herodotus reports that "this change of the day Thales the Milesian had foretold to the Ionians, laying down as a limit this very year in which the change took place," yet the armies stopped fighting because they were frightened by the sudden darkness, not because they understood Thales's prediction. Without using the words "superstition" or "science" directly, explain in your own words how both careful observation and old-fashioned fear of an omen could be operating in the very same historical moment.

assignments.title: 14.11 VR Activity (Supplemental): Map the Six Centuries, Watch Media Move from Vassal to Conqueror
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students explore an animated relief map of the Zagros Mountains and surrounding Near East, watching Median territory and status change across roughly six centuries, from scattered villages to Assyrian tributary to independent empire.

What to do, in order:

  1. Advance the relief map through its marked time stages, watching Median territory and status change.
  2. Compare Media's slow early stages to its rapid later expansion.
  3. Identify the point on the map where Media's trajectory changes most dramatically.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences naming that turning point and explaining why you chose it. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've advanced through all the stages and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Students may expect one obvious turning point. Encourage them to defend their choice with a specific stage on the map rather than guessing.

assignments.title: 14.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Recreate the Battle of the Eclipse
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students stand on a battlefield between Median and Lydian forces as a simulated solar eclipse darkens the sky mid-battle, observing both armies' reaction in real time.

What to do, in order:

  1. Watch the battle unfold between the Median and Lydian forces.
  2. Experience the eclipse's onset as described in this week's Primary Source 2.
  3. Observe both armies halting and moving toward negotiation, then consider how the same event might have felt to a soldier who had never heard of Thales's prediction, compared to one who had.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences comparing those two soldiers' likely reactions. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've watched the eclipse sequence and written your comparison.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): The point is to hold both the real astronomical prediction and the soldiers' fear of an omen as true at once, not to pick one explanation as the real one.

assignments.title: 15.5 Critical Questions: The Legendary Founding of Carthage
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (Dido and the founding of Carthage) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two excerpts from the ancient traditions about Carthage's founding and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 text and to Lesson 1 to reason out your answer.

  1. "[She] directed the hide to be cut into the thinnest possible strips, and thus acquired a greater portion of ground than she had apparently demanded; whence the place had afterwards the name of Byrsa."

    What does this specific detail about the ox hide suggest about the kind of resourcefulness Justin's account wants readers to associate with Dido and her followers?

  2. "Perpetual Hate, and mortal Wars proclaim, / Against the Prince, the People, and the Name," Dido cries, calling for "some Avenger of our Lybian Blood, / With Fire and Sword" to pursue Aeneas's descendants.

    Roman audiences already knew that centuries of war between Rome and Carthage would follow. Using Lesson 1's discussion of why Virgil placed Dido in the wrong historical period on purpose, why might a Roman poet want his audience to believe this rivalry was cursed into existence from this very early, legendary moment?

assignments.title: 15.9 Primary Source Exercise: The Legendary Founding of Rome
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (Romulus and Remus) and Lesson 2.

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. Livy records that Remus received an omen of six vultures, "and now, the omen having been declared, when double the number presented itself to Romulus, his own party saluted each king" instead of the dispute being settled. Suppose the brothers had received a single, undisputed omen and simply agreed which of them should rule. Based on what actually happens next in the text, do you think Rome's own foundation story would have kept the killing in it anyway, or does the ambiguous omen seem necessary to how the Romans told this particular story?

  2. Livy does not soften Rome's founding act of violence: "Remus, in derision of his brother, leaped over his new-built wall, and was, for that reason, slain by Romulus in a passion." Why might a civilization choose to preserve and retell an origin story that makes its own founder look this harsh, rather than inventing a gentler version instead?

assignments.title: 15.10 VR Activity: Two Foundling Cities, Compare Carthage's Harbor and Rome's Hills
assignments.html:
This week's required VR activity.
