Visit two reconstructed environments in sequence: early Carthage, built around its harbor and the hill overlooking it described in Dido's founding legend, and early Rome, built across the Palatine and neighboring hills near the Tiber River where Romulus and Remus are said to have washed ashore.

What you will do: Explore each site's geography first, noting what natural features (a defensible harbor for Carthage, a cluster of easily fortified hills for Rome) made each location a workable choice for a new settlement. Then review a short side-by-side summary of each city's founding legend already covered in this week's Primary Sources.

Time: About 25 minutes.

What to do, in order:

  1. Explore early Carthage's geography, noting the defensible harbor and the hill overlooking it described in Dido's founding legend.
  2. Explore early Rome's geography, noting the Palatine and neighboring hills near the Tiber River where Romulus and Remus are said to have washed ashore.
  3. Review the short side-by-side summary of each city's founding legend, already covered in this week's Primary Sources.
  4. Write a closing response identifying one geographic advantage and one shared story element (exile, hardship, an uncertain beginning) connecting the two cities.
  5. Explain in your own words why neither city's founders could have predicted the rivalry their descendants would eventually inherit.

What to submit: Write a short response identifying one geographic advantage of each site and one story element the two founding legends share (exile, hardship, an uncertain beginning), and explain in your own words why neither city's founders could have predicted the rivalry their descendants would eventually inherit. Submit in Canvas.

You'll know you're done when: You've explored both sites and submitted a response naming a geographic feature and a shared story element for each.

assignments.title: 15.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Sail a Phoenician Trade Route, Purple Dye to Tin
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students crew a simulated Phoenician merchant ship departing Tyre, stopping at a sequence of trading posts across the Mediterranean, loading and unloading representative cargo at each stop.

What to do, in order:

  1. Depart Tyre carrying Tyrian purple dye and cedar goods.
  2. Make stops representing Sicily, Sardinia, and a westernmost post near the Iberian coast, trading for tin and other raw materials at each stop.
  3. Return with a full hold, and identify which leg of the voyage carried the most valuable cargo and why that good was worth the risk of an open-water crossing.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences naming that leg and explaining your reasoning. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've completed the full route and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Tin is the expected answer, given how far west it required sailing to reach, but let students make and defend their own case rather than supplying the answer directly.

assignments.title: 16.5 Critical Questions: Homer's Iliad, Book 1
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (the quarrel of Achilles and Agamemnon) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two excerpts from the opening of the Iliad and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 text and to Lesson 1 to reason out your answer.

  1. "Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans."

    Why might Homer choose to announce the poem's central theme, and its costly consequences, in its very first lines, rather than letting the story unfold before revealing what it is really about?

  2. "Now, therefore, I shall go back to Phthia; it will be much better for me to return home with my ships, for I will not stay here dishonoured to gather gold and substance for you."

    Lesson 2 calls Achilles's withdrawal a vice, a failure of temperance, even while praising his genuine courage as a warrior. Based on this specific quotation, would you agree that Achilles's decision here is more about his own wounded pride than about any larger loyalty to his fellow Greek soldiers? Explain your reasoning.

assignments.title: 16.9 Primary Source Exercise: Homer's Odyssey, Book 9
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (Odysseus and the Cyclops) and Lesson 2.

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. The other Cyclopes ignored Polyphemus's cries for help because he shouted, "Noman is killing me by fraud; no man is killing me by force." What does this detail suggest about how a clever plan's success can depend on details that seem small at the time, in this case, a single word chosen carefully in advance?

  2. Odysseus taunts the blinded Cyclops with his real name and home, "the valiant warrior Ulysses, son of Laertes, who lives in Ithaca," even though this reveals exactly what Polyphemus needs to call down Poseidon's curse on him. Without using the word "irony" directly, explain in your own words how the same clever trick that saves Odysseus's life also sets up the very mistake, his final boast, that causes him lasting trouble.

assignments.title: 16.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Wander a Dark Age Village, How Much Simpler Life Became
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students explore a small, reconstructed Greek village of the Dark Age period, contrasted directly against a reconstructed Mycenaean palace room from Week 8, to see the scale of change firsthand.

What to do, in order:

  1. Walk through the modest Dark Age village, noting its small scale, simple pottery, and lack of monumental architecture or writing.
  2. Switch to the side-by-side view of a Mycenaean palace interior from Week 8 for direct comparison.
  3. List at least two specific differences you observed, and decide which single change (population, literacy, trade, or building scale) you think would have been most keenly felt by someone living through it.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences listing your two differences and naming the change you chose. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've toured both scenes and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Students sometimes describe the difference only in vague terms, like things got worse. Push for the two specific, nameable differences the prompt asks for.

assignments.title: 16.13 VR Activity (Supplemental): Face the Cyclops, Dramatize Odysseus's Escape from Polyphemus's Cave
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students take the role of a member of Odysseus's crew, trapped inside Polyphemus's cave, and act through the key decision points of this week's second Primary Source: offering the wine, giving the false name, and blinding the giant's single eye.

What to do, in order:

  1. Move through the cave environment as a member of Odysseus's crew.
  2. Make the same sequence of choices the text describes: offering the wine, giving the false name, and blinding the giant's eye.
  3. At the final scene, choose whether your character calls out a boastful true name while sailing away or stays silent, then compare your instinct to Homer's account.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences on why you made the choice you did at the end, and what it suggests about the pull toward pride Homer describes. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 15-20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've made all three cave choices and the closing choice, and written your reflection.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): This closing choice is reflective, not graded right or wrong; the text's own outcome is Odysseus boasting. Make sure students know there is no correct choice being scored, only a comparison to reflect on.

assignments.title: 17.5 Critical Questions: The Cyrus Cylinder
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (the Cyrus Cylinder) and Lesson 2.

Directions: Below are two excerpts from the Cyrus Cylinder and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 text and to Lesson 2 to reason out your answer.

  1. "He made him enter his city Babylon without fighting or battle; he saved Babylon from hardship. He delivered Nabonidus, the king who did not revere him, into his hands."

    Why might Cyrus's own inscription want to emphasize that Babylon fell without a fight, rather than describing a hard-won military victory the way Ashurnasirpal II's annals did in Week 11?

  2. "I returned the images of the gods, who had resided there, to their places and I let them dwell in eternal abodes. I gathered all their inhabitants and returned to them their dwellings."

    Lesson 2 says this specific claim is confirmed by outside evidence as real Persian policy, not just royal boasting. Why does this particular detail matter more to a historian than the Cylinder's more general claims about divine favor?

assignments.title: 17.9 Primary Source Exercise: Herodotus on Cyrus's Rise and the Fall of Croesus
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (Cyrus's origins and the fall of Croesus) and Lesson 1.

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. Solon warns Croesus that "before he comes to his end it is well to hold back and not to call him yet happy but only fortunate," since "to many God shows but a glimpse of happiness and then plucks them up by the roots and overturns them." Based on everything else this course has studied about rulers whose fortunes changed suddenly, Naram-Sin, Assyria's rapid collapse, or the Medes' own overthrow by Cyrus, does Solon's warning seem like a special piece of Greek wisdom, or a pattern this course has already been tracking under a different name? Explain your reasoning.

  2. The herdsman ordered to kill the infant Cyrus instead saved him, "substituting his own dead infant, clothing it first in all the other's costly attire," so that Cyrus was raised in secret under a different name. This is now the third time this course has encountered a story about an infant marked for death who instead survives to overthrow the very person who feared him, following Sargon in Week 3 and Romulus and Remus in Week 15. Without simply saying "this happens a lot," explain what specific idea about power, fear, and fate these repeated stories seem to be expressing.

assignments.title: 17.11 VR Activity (Supplemental): Examine the Cyrus Cylinder Up Close, What Does It Actually Claim?
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students examine a life-sized, rotatable model of the Cyrus Cylinder, with sections of its cuneiform text highlighted and paired with plain-language translations drawn from this week's Primary Source 1.

What to do, in order:

  1. Rotate and zoom in on the cylinder to inspect its physical form and cuneiform script.
  2. Step through the highlighted passages one at a time.
  3. Sort each passage into conventional royal boasting or a claim confirmed by outside evidence, then explain, using at least one specific passage, why the same document can contain both kinds of claims.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences giving your example passage and explanation. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've sorted every highlighted passage and written your explanation.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Students sometimes want to sort the whole cylinder into one category or the other. The activity is built to resist that; if asked, remind them the honest answer is that it is genuinely both.

assignments.title: 17.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Compare Empires Side by Side, Assyrian Terror vs. Persian Tolerance
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students stand between two side-by-side scenes, an Assyrian provincial city under Ashurnasirpal-style imperial policy and a Persian provincial city under Cyrus's policy of local autonomy and restored worship, built from material this course studied in Weeks 11 and 17.

What to do, in order:

  1. Walk through the Assyrian provincial city scene, noting the presence or absence of local temples in active use and the visible signs of imperial administration.
  2. Walk through the Persian provincial city scene, making the same observations.
  3. Argue, using at least one specific detail from each scene, whether Assyria's or Persia's approach seems more likely to hold a multi-ethnic empire together over the long run.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences making your argument, citing one detail from each scene. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've toured both scenes and written your argument.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): This question is deliberately left open in Lesson 2. Do not steer students toward a single correct answer; judge the quality of their evidence and reasoning, not which empire they pick.

assignments.title: 18.5 Critical Questions: Herodotus on Cambyses's Conquest of Egypt
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 1 (Cambyses at Pelusium) and Lesson 1.

Directions: Below are two excerpts from Herodotus's account of Cambyses and one question about each. After reading each excerpt, return to the full Primary Source 1 text and to Lesson 1 to reason out your answer.

  1. "Cambyses, like the harebrained person that he was, drew his dagger, and aimed at the belly of the animal, but missed his mark, and stabbed him in the thigh. Then he laughed, and said thus to the priests: 'Oh! blockheads, and think ye that gods become like this, of flesh and blood, and sensible to steel? A fit god indeed for Egyptians, such an one!'"

    Lesson 1 suggests this story likely came from Egyptian sources with reason to resent Cambyses. Does that possibility mean this specific story is definitely false? Explain your reasoning, including what it would take to know for certain either way.

  2. "Apis, wounded in the thigh, lay some time pining in the temple; at last he died of his wound, and the priests buried him secretly without the knowledge of Cambyses."

    What does this detail suggest about the limits of even a conquering king's power over the conquered people's own religious practices, even immediately after a decisive military victory?

assignments.title: 18.9 Primary Source Exercise: The Behistun Inscription
assignments.html:
Covers: Primary Source 2 (the Behistun Inscription) and Lesson 2.

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the text and in what you have learned this week and across this course. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. Darius records that Gaumata "lied to the people, saying: 'I am Smerdis, the son of Cyrus, the brother of Cambyses.' Then were all the people in revolt." What does this detail suggest about how fragile a distant king's authority could be when he was away from the empire's center, as Cambyses was in Egypt?

  2. Lesson 2 argues that the Behistun Inscription's true significance for this course lies less in settling who Gaumata really was and more in its trilingual form. Without using the word "decipherment" directly, explain in your own words why a single inscription written in three different scripts side by side would be more valuable to a future scholar than three separate inscriptions written in only one script each.

assignments.title: 18.10 VR Activity: One Empire, Three River Valleys, Map the Achaemenid Empire
assignments.html:
This week's required VR activity. Work with a large-scale relief map of the ancient Near East, placing and labeling the full extent of the Achaemenid Empire after Cambyses's conquest of Egypt, then marking every earlier civilization this course has studied within or beside it.

What you will do: Starting from a blank relief map showing the Nile, the Tigris-Euphrates, and the Iranian plateau, place labeled markers for Egypt, Mesopotamia, Media, Lydia and Ionia, and Persia's own homeland, then shade the full territory now under a single Achaemenid ruler. Next, place markers for civilizations and peoples this course has studied that lie just outside this empire's current reach, including the Greek mainland city-states, Carthage, and Rome.

Time: About 25 to 30 minutes.

What to do, in order:

  1. Start from the blank relief map showing the Nile, Tigris-Euphrates, and Iranian plateau.
  2. Place labeled markers for Egypt, Mesopotamia, Media, Lydia and Ionia, and Persia's homeland.
  3. Shade the full territory now under a single Achaemenid ruler.
  4. Place markers for civilizations and peoples this course has studied that lie just outside this empire's current reach, including the Greek mainland city-states, Carthage, and Rome.
  5. Write two or three sentences identifying what you think is the single most significant geographic fact about this map.
  6. Name one direction you think this empire is most likely to expand next.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences identifying what you think is the single most significant geographic fact about this map, and name one direction you think this empire is most likely to expand next. Submit in Canvas.

You'll know you're done when: You've placed and shaded all required territories and submitted a closing response naming a geographic fact and a likely direction of expansion.

assignments.title: 18.12 VR Activity (Supplemental): Stand Before the Behistun Cliff
assignments.html:
Supplemental VR activity, optional at your teacher's discretion. Students stand at the base of a reconstructed Mount Behistun cliff face, viewing the carved relief and trilingual inscription high above, then follow a simulated version of Henry Rawlinson's nineteenth-century effort to copy it by hand.

What to do, in order:

  1. Look up at the inscription's height and scale from ground level.
  2. Move along the scaffolded ledge partway up the cliff, taking on Rawlinson's own task of copying sections of the three parallel scripts.
  3. Describe, in your own words, why having the same message in three scripts side by side made this specific climb worth the real risk Rawlinson took.

What to submit: Write two or three sentences with your answer to that closing question. Submit in Canvas.

Time: About 20 minutes.

You'll know you're done when: You've copied the scaffolded sections and written your answer.

Teacher note (remove before publishing to students): Some students will focus only on the physical danger and miss the scholarly payoff, a trilingual key to decipherment. Make sure their written answer addresses why the three scripts mattered, not just the risk.

assignments.title: R.4 Optional Course Review: Tier 3 Comparative Essay
assignments.html:
Focus question: Hammurabi, the kings of Assyria, and Cyrus the Great each tried to bind a large empire together, Hammurabi chiefly through law, Assyria chiefly through the fear of harsh punishment, and Cyrus chiefly through tolerance of conquered peoples' own customs and gods. Using at least two Primary Sources from this course, argue which approach best solved the first-order political and economic problems a large empire faces (keeping internal peace, defending against outside threats, and letting ordinary people trade and prosper), and which approach came at the greatest cost.

Directions:

  1. Choose at least two Primary Sources from this course to support your argument. You may draw from: Hammurabi's law and kingship (the Code of Hammurabi, selected laws, or the Prologue to the Code of Hammurabi, Week 4); Assyria's approach to empire (Ashurnasirpal II's Annals or the Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, Week 11, or Ashurbanipal's Library Tablets, Week 12); or Cyrus's approach to empire (the Cyrus Cylinder, Week 17).
  2. State a clear thesis: which approach, in your judgment, best solved an empire's first-order problems, and which came at the greatest cost. These do not have to be the same approach.
  3. Support your thesis with specific evidence from your chosen Primary Sources, not just general impressions of each ruler.
  4. Address at least one piece of evidence that could complicate or challenge your own argument, and explain why you still find your thesis convincing despite it.
  5. Aim for four to six paragraphs.

Success criteria:

  • Your thesis takes a clear position on both halves of the question (which approach worked best, which cost the most).
  • You quote or closely paraphrase at least two Primary Sources and explain what each one shows.
  • You reason about causes and consequences, not just descriptions of what each ruler did.
  • You acknowledge at least one piece of evidence in tension with your own argument.

Submission instructions: submit as a Word document (.docx).

Before you submit, check that you have:

  • Opened Word from your school Microsoft 365 account, not a personal one.
  • Named your file LastName_FirstName_ComparativeEssay_WH6_Final, using your own name.
  • Saved it in your Optima > History > WorldHistory6 folder in OneDrive.

assignments.html:
Suggested pairing: optional Friday enrichment alongside Week 7, after you have completed that week's lessons.

These questions are open-ended. There is no single correct answer, but your reasoning should be grounded in the appendix reading above and in what you have learned in this course. Quality of reasoning matters more than reaching any particular conclusion.

  1. Week 2 identified dense population, monumental architecture, specialized labor, social stratification, and writing as markers that, appearing together, distinguish a true civilization from a large village. Using evidence from the reading, which of these five markers does Olmec society at San Lorenzo and La Venta clearly show? Which markers are only partly shown, or genuinely uncertain? Explain your reasoning for each.

  2. The Indus Valley civilization, studied in Week 7, has left no royal portrait, no named ruler, and no palace anywhere in its territory. Olmec civilization has left seventeen individually carved stone portraits that most archaeologists believe depict specific rulers, yet not one of those rulers is named. Compare what each civilization's evidence suggests about the presence or absence of kingship, and about the limits of what archaeology alone, without deciphered writing, can tell us about how a civilization was actually governed.

quizzes.description: Welcome to this module. Answer the questions below to get started, then head to Lesson 1 to begin this week's reading.

questions.text: This week's essential question: Was farming really an obvious improvement over foraging? Write down your first answer, before this week's lessons. There is no wrong answer here.
This week you'll study the Neolithic Revolution and the first farming settlements at Jericho and Çatalhöyük. What is one thing you're curious to find out?
Would you be open to being paired with a classmate for optional group discussion or work this module?

answers.text: Yes
No preference
No, I would prefer to work independently

quizzes.title: 1.3 Reading Quiz 1: Why Farm? The Origins of Agriculture

questions.text: A historian argues that early farmers were, in some ways, worse off physically than the foragers who came before them. Based on the lesson, which piece of evidence would best support this argument?

answers.text: Farmers built permanent villages instead of moving seasonally.
Skeletons from early farming villages show more tooth decay and signs of harder labor.
Wild wheat and barley grew across a wide area of the Fertile Crescent.
Sheep and goats were domesticated a few centuries after wheat and barley.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson uses this physical evidence specifically to complicate the assumption that farming was an obvious improvement over foraging.

questions.text: If domesticated wheat and barley were established by roughly 8500 BC, and sheep and goats were domesticated about 500 years later, in approximately what year BC were sheep and goats domesticated?
questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Because BC dates count downward toward the present, 500 years after 8500 BC is 8000 BC, which matches the lesson's stated date for sheep and goat domestication.

questions.text: The lesson states that the Neolithic Revolution unfolded "over dozens of generations" rather than happening quickly. Why does this detail matter for how a historian should describe it?

answers.text: It shows that no single individual or generation can be credited with inventing farming.
It proves that hunter-gatherers were unintelligent and slow to adopt new ideas.
It means the Fertile Crescent was the only place farming ever developed.
It confirms that farming immediately replaced foraging everywhere at once.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson's point about slow, generational change is meant to caution against imagining a single dramatic moment of invention.

questions.text: A community that produces more food than it needs for immediate survival has what the lesson calls a surplus. Based on the lesson, which of the following is a likely long-term consequence of surplus?

answers.text: The community can support people who do not spend all day producing food, such as builders or priests.
The community immediately abandons farming and returns to foraging.
The community's population begins to shrink.
The community loses the ability to survive a bad growing season.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson identifies this as the key downstream consequence of agricultural surplus.

questions.text: The lesson introduces the Six Essential Elements of Geography as a "toolkit" for asking questions about a place. Based on how the lesson uses this toolkit, which question would it help you ask about Jericho?

answers.text: What is the atomic weight of the stone used in Jericho's wall?
How did the people of Jericho and their environment shape one another?
Which country currently claims Jericho as part of its territory?
What is the exact population of Jericho today?

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This reflects the "Environment and Society" element of the Six Essential Elements, which the lesson introduces as a way of connecting people and place, not simply memorizing facts.

quizzes.title: 1.7 Reading Quiz 2: Digging Up the Neolithic: Jericho and Çatalhöyük

questions.text: A mound formed by centuries of people building, abandoning, and rebuilding settlements on the same spot is called what?

answers.text: A ziggurat
A tell
A delta
A plateau

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson defines a tell as exactly this kind of layered mound, and notes that its layers can be read like the pages of a book.

questions.text: Kathleen Kenyon's excavation report describes what she personally found at Jericho in the 1950s. According to the lesson's distinction between primary and secondary sources, in what sense is her report a primary source?

answers.text: It is a firsthand, eyewitness account of the dig itself.
It was written by someone who lived during the Neolithic period.
It contains no interpretation, only raw facts.
It was translated from an ancient language.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson is careful to note that Kenyon's report is primary evidence about the excavation, even though it is only secondary evidence about the Neolithic period itself, since she did not live in that period.

questions.text: The lesson describes Çatalhöyük as a settlement with no streets, where houses were entered through the roof. What does this detail suggest about daily life there?

answers.text: Residents likely traveled between homes by walking across the rooftops.
Residents preferred to live far apart from their neighbors.
The town had wide paved avenues connecting each house.
The town's houses had no roofs at all.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is the direct inference the lesson draws from the rooftop-entry layout.

questions.text: Jericho sits at roughly 31.9 degrees north latitude, and Çatalhöyük sits at roughly 37.7 degrees north latitude. Based on this, which site is located farther north?

answers.text: Jericho
Çatalhöyük
They are at the same latitude.
Latitude cannot tell you this.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: A larger north latitude value means a location farther from the equator, so 37.7 degrees north is farther north than 31.9 degrees north.

questions.text: Regarding the purpose of Jericho's wall and tower, the lesson states that archaeologists are not entirely certain of the builders' motive. What does this uncertainty best illustrate about the practice of archaeology?

answers.text: Archaeologists can sometimes establish clear physical facts while still debating the human motives behind them.
Archaeology can never produce any reliable facts about the ancient world.
Kathleen Kenyon refused to interpret her own evidence.
The wall and tower were definitely built for ceremonial purposes only.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson uses Jericho's wall and tower as a specific example of this gap between established evidence and uncertain interpretation.

questions.text: Revisit this week's essential question: Was farming really an obvious improvement over foraging? Now that you've studied the Neolithic Revolution, Jericho, and Çatalhöyük, has your answer changed? Explain.
How confident do you feel in your understanding of this week's material?

answers.text: Very confident
Somewhat confident
Not very confident
Not confident at all

questions.text: What is one idea, term, or question from this week that still feels unclear to you?
Which virtue (for example: curiosity, patience, honesty, prudence) do you think the people of Neolithic Jericho or Çatalhöyük most needed to build the lives they built? Explain your reasoning.

quizzes.description: Welcome to this module. Answer the questions below to get started, then head to Lesson 1 to begin this week's reading.

quizzes.title: 2.3 Reading Quiz 1: Why Cities? Uruk and the Birth of Urban Life

questions.text: The lesson argues that Sumer's dry climate created a specific first-order economic problem. What was it?

answers.text: Organizing enough people to build and maintain shared irrigation canals.
Finding enough stone to build temples.
Preventing wild animals from destroying crops.
Translating cuneiform tablets accurately.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson identifies this coordination problem as the reason city-states, rather than isolated farms, developed in southern Mesopotamia.

questions.text: Based on the lesson, why were Uruk's earliest rulers described as being "as much accountants as they were kings"?

answers.text: They spent most of their time fighting wars.
They tracked grain, wool, and livestock delivered to and redistributed from the temple.
They were required to personally farm the temple's land.
They had no religious duties at all.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson describes the en/ensi as managing the temple's role as a central storehouse and redistribution hub.

questions.text: Which of the following best reflects the lesson's list of features that mark Uruk as a true civilization rather than simply a large village?

answers.text: A single king with no other officials.
Dense population, monumental architecture, specialized labor, social stratification, and eventually writing, appearing together.
A large population of foragers living without permanent structures.
A population spread evenly across small, identical farms.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is the specific combination of traits the lesson identifies as historians' marker of civilization.

questions.text: According to the lesson, roughly how does the timing of bronze becoming widespread in Mesopotamia (around 3000 BC) compare to the timing of Uruk's rise as a city (around 3450 BC)?

answers.text: Bronze use became widespread several centuries after Uruk had already become a city.
Bronze use became widespread several centuries before Uruk existed.
The two happened in the exact same year.
The lesson does not mention bronze at all.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson places Uruk's rise at approximately 3450 BC and the region's move into the full Bronze Age at approximately 3000 BC, several centuries later.

questions.text: The lesson closes by calling Sumer's temple economy "one particular, historically contingent answer" to the problem of organizing a city, not the only possible one. What is this statement meant to prepare students to notice later in the course?

answers.text: That every ancient civilization organized its economy and government in exactly the same way.
That Egypt, introduced in Week 5, might organize kingship and economy differently than Sumer did.
That Sumer's temple economy was universally regarded as a failure.
That no other civilization ever developed cities.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is a direct forward-looking comparison the lesson sets up rather than stating outright.

quizzes.title: 2.7 Reading Quiz 2: Cuneiform and the Sumerian King List

questions.text: Before true writing developed, Sumerian temple administrators tracked quantities using what method?

answers.text: Small clay tokens shaped like cones, spheres, and disks.
Knotted rope, similar to the Incan quipu.
Carved wooden tally sticks.
Painted pottery designs.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson describes these tokens as the precursor to pressing symbols directly into clay tablets.

questions.text: Based on the lesson, what was the primary early use of cuneiform writing?

answers.text: Recording epic poetry and literature.
Administrative record-keeping, such as tracking grain and livestock.
Writing personal letters between family members.
Recording astronomical observations.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson stresses that literature and history-writing came later, building on a system first developed to solve an accounting problem.

questions.text: According to the Sumerian King List as the lesson describes it, what happens to the length of recorded reigns immediately after the flood?

answers.text: They increase even further beyond the pre-flood lengths.
They remain exactly the same as before the flood.
They disappear from the record entirely.
They shrink toward more plausible, historical lengths.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson notes this shrinkage as a key clue for separating legendary material from material closer to genuine historical memory.

questions.text: The lesson states that Gilgamesh appears both as a real, historical king on the Sumerian King List and as the hero of a legendary epic. What point is this fact meant to illustrate?

answers.text: That the King List and the Epic of Gilgamesh contradict each other so completely that neither can be trusted at all.
That Gilgamesh never actually existed in any form.
That a single ancient figure can be remembered through both administrative record and legendary story at the same time.
That the Epic of Gilgamesh was written before the King List existed.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is the lesson's central point about separating historical memory from legend without dismissing either.

questions.text: Why does the lesson call cuneiform's development a gradual process rather than a single invention?

answers.text: Because tokens, then pressed symbols, then drawn symbols, then true writing, developed over centuries.
Because a single scribe invented the entire system in one afternoon.
Because cuneiform was copied directly from Egyptian hieroglyphics.
Because the Sumerian King List explains exactly how writing was invented.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson traces this multi-stage evolution explicitly.

questions.text: Revisit this week's essential question: Why cities? Now that you've studied Uruk, cuneiform, and the Sumerian King List, has your answer changed? Explain.
How confident do you feel in your understanding of this week's material?

answers.text: Very confident
Somewhat confident
Not very confident
Not confident at all

Which virtue do you think Uruk's temple administrators most needed to keep their city functioning? Explain your reasoning.

questions.text: This week's essential question: Was Sargon's rise to power inevitable, or did it depend on chance? Write down your first answer, before this week's lessons. There is no wrong answer here.

No preference

quizzes.title: 3.3 Reading Quiz 1: A Basket on the River: The Rise of Sargon

questions.text: According to the lesson, what distinguishes an empire from a kingdom?

answers.text: An empire rules many different peoples, cities, and languages at once, often keeping their local customs.
An empire is always smaller in area than a kingdom.
A kingdom always contains more conquered peoples than an empire.
There is no meaningful difference between the two terms.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson draws this distinction explicitly to explain why Sargon's achievement was a genuinely new kind of political problem.

questions.text: Which of the following city-states did Sargon conquer, according to the lesson, defeating its king Lugalzagesi?

answers.text: Jericho
Çatalhöyük
Uruk
Akkad

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson specifically names Uruk and its king Lugalzagesi among Sargon's early conquests, connecting back to Week 2's lesson on Uruk.

questions.text: The lesson calls Sargon's rise from an obscure, basket-borne infant to the ruler of the first empire in history an example of what historical concept?

answers.text: Whiggish history
Contingency
Cyclical determinism
Marxist history

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson explicitly uses the phrase "this is what historians mean by contingency" to describe how Sargon's rise depended on events that did not have to happen.

questions.text: According to the lesson, what happened to Akkad, the capital city Sargon founded?

answers.text: It still exists today under the same name.
It was renamed Uruk after Sargon's death.
It was immediately destroyed by Sargon's own soldiers.
Its exact location has never been rediscovered by archaeologists.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson notes this as a striking detail about how even a capital city can vanish physically while surviving in written memory.

questions.text: Based on the lesson's account of Sargon's path from cupbearer to conqueror, which of the following best describes the sequence of his rise to power?

answers.text: He was born a prince, then became a general, then a cupbearer.
He was elected by the priests of Uruk before conquering Kish.
He was raised by a water-drawer, became a gardener, then rose to cupbearer to the king of Kish, then seized power himself.
He inherited the throne of Akkad directly from his mother.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is the specific sequence the lesson lays out based on the Birth Legend.

quizzes.title: 3.7 Reading Quiz 2: Holding an Empire Together, and Losing It

questions.text: According to the lesson, how did Sargon and his successors try to keep the many conquered cities of their empire functioning together?

answers.text: By leaving every city entirely to its own independent local rulers.
By installing Akkadian-appointed governors and standardizing weights, measures, and administrative practice.
By destroying every conquered city's local government and replacing it with nothing.
By requiring every conquered city to abandon its own language immediately.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is the lesson's description of Akkadian administrative strategy.

questions.text: Naram-Sin, according to the lesson, took which unusual title or status during his reign?

answers.text: "King of the Four Quarters," and, in some traditions, a kind of divine status.
"Drawer of Water"
"Priest of Enlil"
"Servant of Uruk"

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson names this specific title and the extraordinary claim of divine status attached to it.

questions.text: In the Curse of Akkad's own explanation, what triggers Enlil's curse upon Akkad?

answers.text: A drought that Enlil could not prevent.
Naram-Sin's destruction of Enlil's temple, the Ekur, at Nippur.
A rebellion by the Sumerian city-states.
The invention of a new form of writing.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson describes this act of hubris as the poem's central explanation for the curse that follows.

questions.text: Based on the lesson, which of the following best describes how a historian should weigh the Curse of Akkad's religious explanation against modern evidence of drought?

answers.text: The religious explanation should be dismissed entirely in favor of the modern one.
The modern evidence should be dismissed entirely in favor of the religious explanation.
Both explanations likely capture something real about the collapse, without either one being the complete picture.
The two explanations cannot be discussed together in any way.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is the lesson's explicit historiographical point about weighing ancient moral explanations alongside modern material evidence.

questions.text: The lesson closes by connecting Akkad's fall to a later topic in this course. Which topic does it name?

answers.text: The invention of cuneiform in Week 2.
The Bronze Age Collapse in Week 9.
The founding of Rome in Week 15.
The Persian conquest of Egypt in Week 18.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson explicitly previews that this same question about causes of civilizational collapse will return at a larger scale.

questions.text: Revisit this week's essential question: Was Sargon's rise to power inevitable, or did it depend on chance? Now that you've studied Sargon and the Akkadian Empire, has your answer changed? Explain.
How confident do you feel in your understanding of this week's material?

answers.text: Very confident
Somewhat confident
Not very confident
Not confident at all

Naram-Sin's pride is blamed for Akkad's fall in the Curse of Akkad. Which virtue, if Naram-Sin had shown more of it, might have changed the outcome? Explain your reasoning.

quizzes.description: Welcome to this module. Answer the questions below to get started, then head to Lesson 1 to begin this week's reading.

questions.text: This week's essential question: Can a law code be both fair and unfair at once? Write down your first answer, before this week's lessons. There is no wrong answer here.
This week you'll study Hammurabi and his law code. What is one thing you're curious to find out?
Would you be open to being paired with a classmate for optional group discussion or work this module?

answers.text: Yes
No preference
No, I would prefer to work independently

quizzes.title: 4.3 Reading Quiz 1: Amorite Migration and the Rise of Babylon

questions.text: According to the lesson, what did the Amorites generally do upon settling among existing Mesopotamian cities?

answers.text: They destroyed the existing cities and built entirely new ones from scratch.
They largely adopted the existing language, writing system, and religious practices while establishing new ruling dynasties.
They refused any contact with Mesopotamian civilization.
They abandoned city life entirely and returned to nomadic herding.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson stresses that the Amorites stepped into Mesopotamian civilization rather than erasing it.

questions.text: Based on the lesson's account of Hammurabi's reign, when did he complete the military unification of Mesopotamia under Babylon's rule?

answers.text: Immediately upon taking the throne in 1792 BC.
Only late in his reign, in a rapid series of campaigns during his final decade of rule.
He never actually unified Mesopotamia; that was accomplished by his successor.
Exactly halfway through his reign.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson specifically contrasts Hammurabi's decades of cautious, defensive kingship with a late burst of conquest.

questions.text: Which of the following cities does the lesson name among those Hammurabi defeated late in his reign?

answers.text: Jericho and Çatalhöyük
Uruk and Akkad
Larsa, Mari, and Eshnunna
Nineveh and Babylon

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: These are the specific rival cities the lesson names as defeated during Hammurabi's late campaigns.

questions.text: The lesson draws a comparison between Hammurabi's rise and a figure from a previous week. Based on the lesson's discussion of contingency, whose earlier rise does this comparison most resemble?

answers.text: Sargon's improbable rise from an obscure childhood to found the first empire.
Kathleen Kenyon's excavation of Jericho.
The Sumerian King List's account of kingship descending from heaven.
James Mellaart's excavation of Çatalhöyük.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson explicitly draws this contingency parallel, noting that Hammurabi's late-life conquests were far from guaranteed in advance.

questions.text: Why does the lesson caution that Hammurabi's dates (1792 to 1750 BC) are not perfectly settled among historians?

answers.text: Because no ancient records about Hammurabi survive at all.
Because scholars use competing chronological systems, such as the Middle Chronology, that shift ancient Near Eastern dates by decades depending on the evidence given priority.
Because Hammurabi's Code itself contains contradictory dates.
Because Hammurabi ruled for only a single year.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson names the Middle Chronology specifically as the system this course follows, while noting the ongoing scholarly debate.

quizzes.title: 4.7 Reading Quiz 2: Hammurabi's Code: Law, Class, and Kingship

questions.text: According to the lesson, what does lex talionis mean, and what purpose did it serve?

answers.text: "Law of the gods," a rule requiring all disputes to be settled by priests.
"Law of silver," a rule requiring all penalties to be paid in precious metal.
"Law of the king," a rule allowing only the king to punish crimes.
"Law of retaliation," a principle that capped revenge at the same level of harm as the original wrong.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson explains lex talionis specifically as a limiting principle on open-ended revenge.

questions.text: Based on the lesson, how did the Code's penalties for the same injury (such as putting out an eye) differ depending on social class?

answers.text: Penalties were harsher for injuries to an amelu (full free person) and lighter, often a payment, for a mushkenum or a slave.
Penalties were identical regardless of the victim's class.
Only slaves were protected by the Code at all.
The Code did not address personal injury at all.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson describes this as evidence of real, but unequal, justice built into the Code's structure.

questions.text: The lesson connects the Code's precise numeric penalties to which broader Babylonian intellectual achievement?

answers.text: The invention of the alphabet.
A sophisticated mathematics built on a sexagesimal (base-60) number system, including Plimpton 322.
The domestication of sheep and goats.
The construction of the pyramids.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson draws this direct connection between legal precision and mathematical sophistication.

questions.text: Which of the following best reflects the lesson's overall evaluation of the Code's justice?

answers.text: The Code was entirely just and applied with perfect equality to everyone.
The Code was entirely unjust and offered no real protection to anyone.
The Code offered real, predictable, publicly known justice while also building inequality directly into its structure, and a fair evaluation must hold both truths at once.
The Code addressed only religious matters and had nothing to do with justice.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is the lesson's explicit, balanced evaluation.

questions.text: According to the lesson, how does Hammurabi justify his own right to rule in the Code's prologue?

answers.text: By claiming that only military force determines who deserves to rule.
By presenting himself as chosen by the gods to make justice prevail and protect the weak from the strong.
By claiming direct descent from Sargon of Akkad.
By arguing that kingship is unnecessary in a well-run society.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson identifies this as the standard Hammurabi sets for his own rule, one that can be measured against his actual conduct.

questions.text: Revisit this week's essential question: Can a law code be both fair and unfair at once? Now that you've studied Hammurabi's Code, has your answer changed? Explain.
How confident do you feel in your understanding of this week's material?

answers.text: Very confident
Somewhat confident
Not very confident
Not confident at all

questions.text: What is one idea, term, or question from this week that still feels unclear to you?
Hammurabi's prologue claims justice as the standard for his own rule. Which virtue does a ruler need most to actually live up to a promise like that? Explain your reasoning.

quizzes.title: 5.1 Module Check-In: Start of Module
quizzes.description: Welcome to this module. Answer the questions below to get started, then head to Lesson 1 to begin this week's reading.

questions.text: This week's essential question: Why did Egypt unify almost overnight, while Mesopotamia took centuries? Write down your first answer, before this week's lessons. There is no wrong answer here.
This week you'll study Narmer, Egypt's Old Kingdom, and the Great Pyramid. What is one thing you're curious to find out?
Would you be open to being paired with a classmate for optional group discussion or work this module?

answers.text: Yes
No preference
No, I would prefer to work independently

questions.text: According to the lesson, why could Nile farmers generally count on their harvest in a way Mesopotamian farmers could not always rely on?

answers.text: Egypt received more rainfall directly than Mesopotamia did.
The Nile flooded on a far more predictable yearly schedule than the Tigris and Euphrates did.
Egyptian farmers used irrigation canals while Mesopotamian farmers did not.
The Nile never flooded at all, so farmers never worried about water.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson contrasts the Nile's regular, expected flood cycle with the Tigris and Euphrates' less predictable flooding.

questions.text: The lesson states that agriculture in Egypt originated:

answers.text: At the same time as Sumerian agriculture, through direct trade contact.
In the Nile Delta first, then spread south to Upper Egypt.
In the Fertile Crescent, then spread to the Nile Valley by around 5200 BC.
Independently, with no connection to any other region.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson makes clear that Egypt imported agriculture rather than inventing it independently.

questions.text: What event does the Narmer Palette commemorate, according to the lesson?

answers.text: The founding of the city of Memphis by a council of priests.
A trade agreement between Upper and Lower Egypt.
A peace treaty ending a war between Egypt and Mesopotamia.
The unification of Upper and Lower Egypt under one crown.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson identifies the Palette with Narmer's unification of the two lands around 3100 BC.

questions.text: How does the lesson describe the relationship between Egyptian kingship and Mesopotamian kingship?

answers.text: Egyptian kings were treated as living gods from a very early point, while Mesopotamian kingship developed more gradually, often still tied to priesthoods.
Both developed in exactly the same way, with no meaningful differences.
Mesopotamian kings were considered gods, while Egyptian pharaohs were not considered divine at all.
Neither Egypt nor Mesopotamia connected kingship to religion in any way.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson draws this comparison directly as a genuine difference in how the two civilizations understood royal authority.

questions.text: Why does the lesson suggest that Egypt's geography may have made rapid, total unification under one divine king more achievable than in Mesopotamia?

answers.text: Egypt had no deserts at all, making travel between regions instantaneous.
Mesopotamia had no rivers at all, making unification there impossible.
Egypt's isolation between deserts gave a unifying king less external competition to answer to than a Mesopotamian ruler surrounded by rival cities.
Egypt had far more rainfall than Mesopotamia, requiring no centralized irrigation planning.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson offers this geographic contrast as part, though not all, of an explanation for Egypt's different pattern of kingship.

quizzes.title: 5.7 Reading Quiz 2: The Old Kingdom: Pyramids, Labor, and Wisdom

questions.text: What does archaeological evidence from workers' villages near the pyramids suggest about who built the Great Pyramid?

answers.text: A workforce that included organized, provisioned laborers, some rotating seasonally and some skilled and permanent, rather than mass slavery.
A small group of fewer than one hundred elite priests.

It was destroyed by Sargon's own soldiers shortly after being built
Its exact location has never been rediscovered by archaeologists, despite Akkad's fame in ancient records

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Even a capital city can vanish physically while surviving in written memory.

questions.text: How did Sargon and his successors try to keep the many conquered cities of their empire functioning together as one political unit?

answers.text: By leaving every conquered city entirely to its own independent local rulers, with no central oversight
By installing Akkadian-appointed governors and standardizing weights, measures, and administrative practice across conquered territory
By destroying every conquered city's local government and replacing it with nothing at all
By requiring every conquered city to abandon its own spoken language immediately

questions.text: When Amorite migrants settled among the existing cities of Mesopotamia, what did they generally do once they had established new ruling dynasties?

answers.text: They destroyed the existing cities entirely and built new ones from scratch
They largely adopted the existing language, writing system, and religious practices already established in Mesopotamia
They refused any contact whatsoever with Mesopotamian civilization
They abandoned city life entirely and returned to nomadic herding

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The Amorites, including Hammurabi's own dynasty, stepped into Mesopotamian civilization rather than erasing it.

questions.text: Under the Code of Hammurabi, how did the penalty for the same injury, such as putting out an eye, typically differ depending on the social class of the victim?

answers.text: Penalties were identical no matter the victim's social class
Only slaves were protected by the Code at all
Penalties were harsher when the victim was a full free person (amelu), and often reduced to a payment when the victim was a commoner (mushkenum) or a slave
The Code did not address personal injury of any kind

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This class-based difference is evidence of real, but unequal, justice built into the Code's own structure.

questions.text: Considered as a whole, how should a historian fairly evaluate the justice offered by the Code of Hammurabi?

answers.text: The Code was entirely just and applied with perfect equality to every person
The Code was entirely unjust and offered no real protection to anyone at all
The Code addressed only religious matters and had nothing to do with justice
The Code offered real, predictable, publicly known justice, while also building inequality directly into its own structure, so a fair evaluation must hold both truths at once

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This balanced judgment reflects the course's Classical Republican approach to evaluating ancient law.

questions.text: Why could farmers along the Nile generally count on their harvest in a way that farmers along the Tigris and Euphrates could not always rely on?

answers.text: Egypt received far more direct rainfall than Mesopotamia did
The Nile flooded on a far more predictable yearly schedule than the Tigris and Euphrates did
Egyptian farmers used irrigation canals, while Mesopotamian farmers used none at all
The Nile never flooded at all, so farmers there never had to plan around flooding

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This predictability is a key geographic difference behind Egypt's distinct pattern of kingship and stability.

questions.text: What does archaeological evidence from workers' villages near the Great Pyramid suggest about the people who actually built it?

answers.text: A workforce made up entirely of foreign prisoners of war
Machines and animals performed nearly all of the labor, with almost no human workers involved
A small group of fewer than one hundred elite priests
An organized, provisioned workforce, some workers rotating seasonally and others skilled and permanent, rather than a mass of enslaved laborers

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Evidence from bakeries, breweries, and housing near the pyramid corrects the popular myth of mass slave labor.

questions.text: What kind of text is the Instructions of Ptahhotep?

answers.text: A royal law code listing crimes and their punishments
A military account describing a pharaoh's battles
A wisdom text offering a vizier's practical advice on virtues such as patience, courtesy, and listening well
A religious hymn praising the sun god Ra

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: It models personal virtue rather than issuing monumental royal decrees.

questions.text: What military technology is credited to the Hyksos, who ruled part of Egypt before the New Kingdom, and which later New Kingdom armies relied on heavily?

answers.text: Cuneiform writing
Irrigation canals
The wheel and pottery
The horse-drawn chariot and the composite bow

questions.text: Why did Egypt need a reliable, ongoing source of incense, myrrh, and similar goods from the land of Punt?

Egypt could produce these goods domestically, but simply preferred variety
Punt paid Egypt tribute in these goods, so no expedition was ever necessary

questions.text: Beyond its outcome, what makes the surviving account of the Battle of Megiddo especially significant to historians?

answers.text: It is the only ancient Egyptian military record that has ever been found
It describes a battle that Egypt actually lost
It is the earliest battle in world history for which a detailed, specific account survives
It was written by a Mesopotamian scribe rather than an Egyptian one

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is why historians treat Thutmose III's Megiddo campaign as a landmark source, not only a military victory.

questions.text: What feature of Mohenjo-daro's urban planning is considered unusually advanced for its time?

answers.text: A single enormous royal palace at the city's center
A massive defensive wall built specifically to withstand chariot attacks
A large temple complex dedicated to one named god
A precise street grid, standardized bricks, and covered drains, along with private wells and bathing rooms

questions.text: What genuine, still-unresolved puzzle do historians identify about Indus Valley civilization?

answers.text: No cities have ever been found anywhere in the Indus Valley
No royal palace, grand temple, or named ruler has ever been identified there, despite careful excavation
The Indus civilization is confirmed to have had no writing system whatsoever
Archaeologists have found extensive evidence of large-scale warfare between Indus cities

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is presented as a real, open question rather than a settled fact.

questions.text: What are oracle bones, as used in Shang China?

Building bricks used in the construction of the city of Anyang

questions.text: What likely makes the Battle of Kadesh, fought between Egypt and the Hittite Empire, especially notable in military history?

It ended in the total destruction of the Egyptian army
It was fought between two rival Mesopotamian city-states
It was likely the largest chariot battle ever fought in world history

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Kadesh's scale, not a clear victory for either side, is its key historical distinction.

questions.text: What genuine, unresolved puzzle do historians identify about the Minoan palace at Knossos?

answers.text: No trace of the palace has ever been found by archaeologists
Knossos had no plumbing or water management system of any kind
Unlike nearly every other major Bronze Age capital, Knossos was built with no defensive walls at all
Knossos was built entirely underground

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This remains a genuinely debated puzzle, not a settled fact.

questions.text: The ruler at the head of a Mycenaean palace's hierarchy was called the wanax. What do the Linear B tablets, produced by that palace bureaucracy, overwhelmingly record?

answers.text: Poetry and religious hymns
Personal letters exchanged between Mycenaean kings
Numbers, such as sheep, chariots, grain, and land, tracked for palace bookkeeping
Detailed law codes similar to Hammurabi's

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Linear B's surviving content is overwhelmingly administrative, not literary.

questions.text: What does Merneptah's victory stele, commemorating his fight against a Libyan and Sea Peoples coalition around 1208 BC, contain that makes it especially significant to historians of the ancient Levant?

The first confirmed reference to the Sumerian King List
A detailed account of the Battle of Kadesh
The earliest surviving reference to Phoenician trade

A detailed personal narrative of the palace's destruction, preserved on papyrus
Poetry describing the palace's final battle, preserved by being copied onto Linear A tablets

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The same fire that ended Pylos accidentally preserved the record of its final days.

questions.text: Following the Bronze Age Collapse, which civilization was positioned to inherit much of the long-distance Mediterranean trade network that Mycenaean sailors had once run?

answers.text: The Hittite Empire
The Indus Valley civilization
Shang China
Phoenicia

He remained in Egypt permanently to govern every region directly.
He immediately declared war on Assyria.

quizzes.title: 10.7 Reading Quiz 2: Herodotus, and a Dynasty That Looked Backward

questions.text: Why does the lesson call Herodotus the "Father of History"?

answers.text: Because he was the very first person in any culture to ever write about the past.
Because his account of Egypt contains no errors of any kind.
Because he approached the past by traveling to see things himself, questioning multiple sources, and openly noting his own uncertainty.
Because he ruled Egypt during the Saite period.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson credits this method, not simply being first to write, as the reason for the title.

questions.text: What does the lesson say about how Herodotus should be read?

answers.text: With complete, uncritical trust in every claim he makes.
With complete rejection, since nothing he reports is considered reliable.
Only as poetry, never as a historical source.
With care, distinguishing his plausible eyewitness reporting from stories he passes along while openly doubting them.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson uses the phoenix story specifically to illustrate this distinction.

questions.text: What does the lesson say was distinctive about how the Saite pharaohs approached Egyptian art and architecture?

answers.text: They deliberately studied and imitated Old Kingdom styles and inscriptions from nearly a thousand years earlier.
They copied Mesopotamian styles exclusively.
They rejected all earlier Egyptian styles and invented something entirely new.
They stopped building monuments altogether.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson presents this as a deliberate choice to look backward for legitimacy.

questions.text: According to the lesson, what point does the Saite revival illustrate about how history actually moves?

answers.text: That history always moves forward toward improvement.
That civilizations never change their artistic styles.
That the Saite pharaohs had no knowledge of Egypt's earlier dynasties.
That a civilization can deliberately look to its own past rather than always moving forward, contradicting any inevitable, one-directional view of history.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson uses this directly to push back against any assumption that history always moves forward.

questions.text: What does the lesson identify as the timing relationship between Herodotus's visit and the Saite period?

answers.text: Herodotus visited centuries before the Saite period began.
Herodotus likely visited during or shortly after the Saite period, helping explain how much he was able to see and record.
Herodotus never actually visited Egypt in person.
The Saite period began only after Herodotus's death.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson connects this timing directly to the quality of his account.

It was written entirely in a single, well-known language.
