questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson compares its role to the Rosetta Stone's role in deciphering hieroglyphics.

questions.text: What did Henry Rawlinson do in the 1830s and 1840s, according to the lesson?

answers.text: He led a military campaign to conquer the region around Mount Behistun.
He repeatedly risked his life scaling the cliff face to copy the inscription by hand.
He translated the inscription without ever visiting the site.
He destroyed the inscription after copying a small portion of it.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson credits this work with eventually unlocking Babylonian cuneiform.

questions.text: What does the lesson identify as new about the Achaemenid Empire by the end of this week's story?

answers.text: It had lost control of Mesopotamia entirely.
It had shrunk back to its original Persian homeland only.
For the first time, Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Persia's own homeland all answered to one empire, which now looked toward Greece.
It had merged completely with the Ionian Greek city-states.

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The lesson closes this course's narrative arc on this point.

questions.text: Revisit this week's essential question: One Empire, Three River Valleys: What Comes Next for Greece? Now that you've studied Cambyses's conquest of Egypt and Darius's rise, has your answer changed? Explain.
How confident do you feel in your understanding of this week's material?

answers.text: Very confident
Somewhat confident
Not very confident
Not confident at all

questions.text: What is one idea, term, or question from this week that still feels unclear to you?

This week closes out this course's story, from Sumer's first cities to one empire ruling Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Persia's own homeland together. Herodotus portrays Cambyses as unstable and impious, while Darius carved his own justification in stone for anyone to read. Looking back across these eighteen weeks, which virtue, or its absence, does this closing chapter of rulers and power raise most clearly for you? Explain your reasoning.
Before Piye's Kushite conquest, Egypt's Third Intermediate Period is best described by which of the following?

answers.text: A kingdom already fully controlled by Assyria
A land completely abandoned by its population
A single unified kingdom stronger than any earlier period
A kingdom that had drifted apart into rival dynasties, local princes, and powerful Theban priests, rather than collapsing all at once

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This slow political drift, not a single dramatic event, describes Egypt in this period.

questions.text: What event, occurring not long after Piye's conquest, severely weakened the Kushite Twenty-fifth Dynasty's hold on Egypt?

answers.text: A famine along the Nile
An internal rebellion among Kushite nobles
The Assyrian sack of Thebes in 663 BC
A peace treaty with the Hittites

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This shock was severe enough that a prophet could still invoke it as a warning more than a century later.

questions.text: The Saite pharaohs, who ruled Egypt after the Kushite period, deliberately studied and imitated art and inscriptions from nearly a thousand years earlier. What does this choice illustrate about how history actually moves?

answers.text: That history always moves forward toward improvement
That civilizations never change their artistic styles at all
That a civilization can deliberately look back to its own past rather than always moving forward, against any assumption that history marches in one direction
That the Saite pharaohs had no knowledge of Egypt's earlier dynasties

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: The Saite revival is a direct example against Whiggish, one-directional history.

questions.text: How is Ashurnasirpal II's well-documented violence against rebellious cities best characterized?

answers.text: As deliberate, publicized state policy meant to terrorize potential rebels into submission
As random, uncontrolled cruelty with no larger purpose
As entirely fabricated by later, hostile writers
As a private matter kept hidden from the public

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: These acts were carved and displayed rather than hidden.

questions.text: What term describes a ruler who keeps his own throne, but only by paying tribute and submitting to a stronger power, as Jehu of Israel did toward Assyria?

answers.text: Pharaoh
Ensi
Vassal
Satrap

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is the term introduced to describe Jehu's relationship to Shalmaneser III.

questions.text: What did paying tribute to a stronger empire allow a smaller kingdom like Israel to do, even at a real cost?

answers.text: Completely avoid any relationship with the larger empire
Immediately conquer the larger empire in return
Avoid ever having to interact with that empire again
Preserve its own existence, even though doing so meant giving up full independence

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Tribute was a practical strategy for a smaller kingdom facing overwhelming force.

questions.text: What unusual claim did Ashurbanipal make about his own upbringing, one considered highly unusual for a Mesopotamian king?

answers.text: That he never learned to read at all
That he was personally taught to read and write cuneiform as a young prince, a skill normally reserved for trained scribes
That he personally invented cuneiform writing
That he abolished the position of scribe throughout his empire

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This claim of personal literacy sets Ashurbanipal apart from most Mesopotamian kings.

questions.text: What is a colophon, as found on tablets from Ashurbanipal's library?

answers.text: A short scribal note identifying a tablet's owner, sometimes warning against its removal or damage
A type of Assyrian weapon
A Babylonian unit of currency
A title given only to foreign kings

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: One surviving example invokes the gods' anger against anyone who might steal the tablet.

questions.text: According to this course's Classical Republican, Hegel-influenced historiographical lens, what does war serve as "the ultimate test" of?

answers.text: A civilization's artistic achievements
A king's ability to read and write
A state's capacity to organize against external threats, since that capacity cannot be faked with propaganda alone
A kingdom's religious devotion only

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Assyria's sudden collapse after Ashurbanipal's death is the course's sharpest example of a state failing this test.

questions.text: What empire rose in Mesopotamia to fill the vacuum left by Assyria's sudden collapse after the fall of Nineveh?

answers.text: The Neo-Babylonian Empire, under Nebuchadnezzar II
The Median Empire
A restored Neo-Assyrian Empire
The Achaemenid Empire

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Babylon, one of the two powers that had destroyed Nineveh, entered its own most famous and powerful period afterward.

questions.text: How does Israelite religion, centered on one god and a covenant with the Israelite people, compare to the polytheistic systems studied earlier in this course, such as those of Mesopotamia and Egypt?

answers.text: It is a genuinely distinct religious commitment worth understanding on its own terms, not simply another version of the same polytheistic pattern
It is essentially identical, just with different names for the same gods
It has no connection to any historical events at all
It is identical to the Egyptian concept of ma'at

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This comparison is treated as a genuine difference in commitments, not flattened into equivalence.

questions.text: What does the persistence of Israelite identity through decades of exile in Babylon, without a king, a temple, or a homeland, suggest to historians?

answers.text: That such identity disappeared completely into the wider Babylonian population
That this was an inevitable, guaranteed outcome with no real uncertainty involved
That this outcome was genuinely unusual and not something that had to happen
That the exiles had already returned home before the exile technically began

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This persistence through exile is treated as a real historical surprise, not a foregone conclusion.

questions.text: For roughly four centuries, from about 1150 to 728 BC, how do the Medes appear in the surviving historical record?

answers.text: They left behind detailed royal inscriptions just like Assyria and Egypt did
They ruled a large, well-documented empire during this entire period
They are completely unmentioned in any ancient source whatsoever
They appear only faintly and occasionally, mostly as a tribute-paying people along Assyria's frontier

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is a genuine gap in the surviving record, not evidence that nothing was happening among the Medes.

questions.text: According to Herodotus, how did Deioces first gain authority among the Medes, in a notably different origin story from most kingdoms studied earlier in this course?

answers.text: Through a reputation for fair judgment that led people from beyond his own village to bring him their disputes
Through military conquest of neighboring villages
Through inheriting the position directly from his father
Through a treaty signed with Assyria

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This origin story stands apart from the conquest-driven rises of Sargon or Hammurabi.

questions.text: What irony closes the story of Cyaxares, the Median king who helped destroy Nineveh in 612 BC?

answers.text: His royal line ruled successfully for many centuries afterward with no challenge
His own royal line was overthrown within a few decades by his own grandson, a figure this course studies in Week 17
His line was destroyed by Lydia shortly after making peace with it
His line merged peacefully with the Assyrian royal line

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This detail directly previews Cyrus's own rise.

questions.text: Why did the Phoenician alphabet spread so quickly compared to cuneiform or hieroglyphics?

answers.text: It used only about twenty-two simple symbols, far fewer than the hundreds needed for cuneiform or hieroglyphics
It was the only writing system anyone in the Mediterranean had ever seen
It could only be read by trained priests, which made it more prestigious
It was invented by the Greeks and then borrowed by Phoenicia

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This simplicity let merchants, not only scribes, learn and carry it from port to port.

questions.text: How did Nebuchadnezzar II's thirteen-year siege of the Phoenician city of Tyre actually end?

answers.text: Tyre was completely destroyed, the same way Jerusalem was
Nebuchadnezzar abandoned the siege and Tyre remained fully independent
Tyre's king was executed and replaced with a Babylonian governor
The siege ended in negotiated terms, with Tyre acknowledging Babylonian overlordship while keeping its own king, walls, and fleet

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Tyre survived through being valuable rather than through military strength.

questions.text: According to Livy, what caused the fatal quarrel between Romulus and Remus after they had already survived being abandoned as infants?

answers.text: A disagreement over which twin their grandfather Numitor favored
A disagreement over who would marry first
A disagreement over exactly where their new city's wall and sacred boundary should be marked
A dispute over which twin had been born first

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Romulus killed Remus after Remus mockingly leaped over the boundary line.

questions.text: What happened to Linear B literacy after the Mycenaean palaces collapsed?

answers.text: It became even more widely used by ordinary Greek villagers
It vanished entirely, and Greece became functionally illiterate for roughly three centuries
It was replaced immediately by the Phoenician alphabet
It continued to be used only within a small circle of former palace scribes

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Linear B had only ever been taught to specially trained palace scribes, so it disappeared along with the palaces.

questions.text: What development, beginning around 800 BC, let Greek communities read and write again after their long Dark Age illiteracy?

answers.text: The invention of cuneiform
The rediscovery of Linear B
Greek communities adopting and adapting the Phoenician alphabet, adding vowel signs of their own
The spread of hieroglyphics to Greece

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This adoption is a direct payoff of Phoenicia's own writing-technology spotlight from Week 15.

questions.text: What does the *Iliad* suggest Achilles's withdrawal from battle actually costs the Greek army?

answers.text: Nothing of consequence, since the Greeks win the war regardless
Only Achilles's own personal reputation, with no wider consequences
It costs Agamemnon his position as commander
It costs the Greeks dearly, since the poem is explicit that this decision, not any single battle, brings real harm

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is treated as a study in destructive, unchecked pride.

questions.text: According to Herodotus, what did King Astyages fear about his own grandson, and what did he attempt to do about it?

answers.text: He feared a foreign invasion and built new fortifications
He feared his grandson Cyrus, and ordered the infant killed
He feared Lydia and formed an alliance against it
He feared a famine and ordered grain stockpiled

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: A herdsman spared the child instead, setting up Cyrus's later rise.

questions.text: What warning did Solon reportedly give King Croesus of Lydia, a warning later connected to Croesus's eventual defeat?

answers.text: That Croesus should attack Persia immediately while he still could
That Croesus's wealth was fake and had been exaggerated
That no man should be counted happy until his life has actually ended, since fortune can turn on anyone
That Solon himself planned to seize the Lydian throne

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This warning is connected directly to Croesus's later fall.

questions.text: What specific policy of Cyrus's actual rule is treated as genuinely significant, regardless of how conventional the Cyrus Cylinder's own language may otherwise be?

answers.text: Returning displaced peoples to their home cities and restoring their gods' images to their proper shrines
Building an entirely new capital city from scratch
Requiring all conquered peoples to worship Marduk exclusively
Abolishing local languages across the empire

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This real policy, not the Cylinder's conventional language alone, connects directly to the Judean exiles' return.

questions.text: What became genuinely new about the ancient Near East once Cambyses defeated Psamtik III at Pelusium in 525 BC?

answers.text: Persia had already controlled Egypt for centuries before this
Egypt became fully independent from all outside powers
For the first time in this course's story, Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Persia's own homeland were bound under a single empire
Mesopotamia and Egypt merged into a single culture with no Persian involvement

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This union of three river-valley regions had never quite happened before.

questions.text: What makes the Behistun Inscription's physical form especially significant to historians, in a way that helped later scholars decipher a lost script?

answers.text: It is the longest inscription ever discovered in the ancient Near East
It was carved on a portable object rather than a cliff face
It was written entirely in a single, well-known language
It presents the same text in three languages and scripts: Old Persian, Elamite, and Babylonian

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Its trilingual form played a role in unlocking cuneiform, similar to the Rosetta Stone's role with hieroglyphics.

questions.text: What did the scholar Henry Rawlinson do in the 1830s and 1840s that eventually helped unlock Babylonian cuneiform?

answers.text: He translated the inscription without ever visiting the site
He repeatedly risked his life scaling a cliff face to copy the Behistun Inscription by hand
He led a military campaign to conquer the region around Mount Behistun
He destroyed the inscription after copying a small portion of it

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This dangerous, painstaking work eventually helped unlock Babylonian cuneiform for modern scholars.

quizzes.title: R.2 Optional Course Review: Tier 1 Quiz

questions.text: Çatalhöyük sits at roughly 37.7°N latitude, and Jericho at roughly 31.9°N. Which site lies farther north?

answers.text: Jericho
Çatalhöyük
The two sites are at the same latitude
Latitude alone cannot answer this question

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: A higher latitude number means a site is farther from the equator, and 37.7°N is farther north than 31.9°N.

questions.text: Before true writing developed, Sumerian temple administrators tracked quantities of grain and livestock using which method?

answers.text: Small clay tokens, such as cones, spheres, and disks
Knotted rope
Wooden tally sticks
Painted pottery marks

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This token system is the direct ancestor of the wedge-shaped cuneiform writing that followed it.

questions.text: Legend describes Sargon of Akkad's rise to power following which sequence?

answers.text: Born a prince, then made a general, then crowned king
Elected directly by the priests of Uruk
Raised as the son of a water-drawer, worked as a gardener, then became cupbearer to the king of Kish before seizing power himself
Inherited Akkad's throne directly from his mother

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This unlikely path is central to why Sargon's rise is treated as a case of historical contingency.

questions.text: Sargon's grandson, Naram-Sin, took which unusual title or status during his reign?

answers.text: "King of the Four Quarters," and in some traditions divine status
"Drawer of Water"
"Priest of Enlil"
"Servant of Uruk"

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Naram-Sin's elevated claims stand in contrast to his empire's eventual collapse, one of this course's earliest lessons in historiography.

questions.text: Late in his reign, Hammurabi of Babylon defeated which rival cities to unify southern Mesopotamia under his rule?

answers.text: Jericho and Çatalhöyük
Uruk and Akkad
Larsa, Mari, and Eshnunna
Nineveh and Babylon

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: These conquests came after decades of Hammurabi ruling a smaller kingdom, completing his unification of southern Mesopotamia.

questions.text: The principle of lex talionis in Hammurabi's Code means "law of retaliation." What purpose did it serve?

answers.text: It let priests alone decide every dispute
It required all penalties to be paid in silver
It reserved all punishment to the king personally
It capped revenge at the level of the original wrong, rather than allowing unlimited retaliation

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is one reason Hammurabi's Code is treated as evidence of stable, publicly recognized law.

questions.text: The Narmer Palette is understood to commemorate which event?

answers.text: The founding of Memphis by priests
A trade agreement between Upper and Lower Egypt
A peace treaty between Egypt and Mesopotamia
The unification of Upper and Lower Egypt under one crown

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This unification, traditionally dated to around 3100 BC, anchors the start of Egypt's long dynastic history.

questions.text: The Great Pyramid at Giza was completed under which pharaoh, and in roughly what period?

answers.text: Narmer, around 3100 BC
Hammurabi, around 1792 BC
Ramesses III, around 1250 BC
Khufu, around 2560 BC

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Placing this date correctly requires keeping Egypt's Old Kingdom timeline separate from Mesopotamia's later rulers.

questions.text: Hatshepsut expanded Egypt's wealth chiefly through a major trading and diplomatic expedition to the land of Punt, while her successor Thutmose III expanded Egypt's territory chiefly through repeated military campaigns into the Levant, most famously at Megiddo. Which statement best describes their two approaches?

answers.text: Hatshepsut pursued prosperity through diplomacy and trade, while Thutmose III pursued expansion through military conquest, and neither approach was clearly superior to the other
Both rulers relied entirely on military conquest, differing only in which enemy they attacked
Hatshepsut's reign achieved nothing of lasting value compared to Thutmose III's conquests
Thutmose III abandoned all of Hatshepsut's policies immediately upon taking the throne

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Both paths solved Egypt's first-order political and economic problems in genuinely different ways.

questions.text: Fu Hao, known from Shang oracle bone inscriptions, is best identified as which of the following?

answers.text: The legendary flood-taming founder of the Xia dynasty
The diviner who invented oracle bone script
A consort of King Wu Ding whose inscriptions describe her personally leading military campaigns
A queen of the Indus Valley civilization

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Fu Hao is one of the best-documented women commanding armies anywhere in the ancient world.

questions.text: After years of tension following the Battle of Kadesh, Egypt and the Hittite Empire ultimately took which step?

answers.text: They concluded a formal peace treaty, with mutual promises of non-aggression and defense
They fought a second, decisive battle that ended the conflict
Egypt absorbed the Hittite empire outright
The Hittites absorbed Egypt outright

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This treaty, one of this course's Primary Sources, is among the earliest surviving international peace agreements.

questions.text: Historians generally explain the Bronze Age Collapse using which kind of explanation?

answers.text: A single, clearly proven cause historians agree on
A currency crisis alone
A deliberate, coordinated invasion planned years in advance
A combination of drought, internal political failure, and disrupted trade networks, reinforcing one another

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This "systems collapse" explanation avoids pinning the collapse on any single villain.

questions.text: Which of the following did NOT survive the Bronze Age Collapse as a continuing political power?

answers.text: Egypt
Mesopotamia generally
The Hittite Empire
Phoenicia's coastal trading cities

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Unlike Egypt, which survived wounded, or Phoenicia, which went on to inherit Mycenaean trade routes, the Hittite state did not continue.

questions.text: Piye of Kush ruled a kingdom located along the upper Nile, to the south of Egypt. What was Kush's relationship to Egyptian religious tradition?

answers.text: Kush had no connection to Egyptian religious practice
Kush had absorbed Egyptian religious practice so thoroughly that its kings saw themselves as guardians of it
Kush practiced an entirely Greek religion
Kush was religiously indistinguishable from the Nile Delta but politically separate

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is part of why Piye's conquest of Egypt is presented as restoration rather than foreign invasion in his own inscriptions.

questions.text: Herodotus is often called the "Father of History." Why?

answers.text: He was the first person in any culture ever to write about the past
He traveled to see things himself, questioned multiple sources, and openly noted his own uncertainty
His account of Egypt contains no factual errors
He personally ruled Egypt during the Saite period

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This method, not perfect accuracy, is why his approach is treated as a genuine historical method rather than simple legend-telling.

questions.text: Sumer and Akkad's armies, earlier in this course's story, were built mainly from seasonal levies, farmers called up for a campaign and then returned to their fields. How did Assyria's military system differ by the height of its empire?

answers.text: Assyria abandoned standing armies entirely and relied only on hired foreign mercenaries
Assyria's army remained a seasonal levy system, unchanged from Sumerian and Akkadian practice
Assyria moved toward a professional, standing army equipped with iron weapons, siege engineering, and cavalry, kept under arms year-round
Assyria fought exclusively with chariots and fielded no infantry at all

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This shift helps explain Assyria's capacity to dominate the Near East for centuries.

questions.text: Why is the Black Obelisk's depiction of Jehu of Israel especially significant to historians?

answers.text: It is the only surviving Assyrian monument of any kind
It is one of the very few surviving ancient images of a specific, named Israelite king
It proves that Jehu defeated Shalmaneser III in battle
It was created by Israelite, not Assyrian, artists

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This makes it an unusually direct point of contact between Assyrian and Israelite history.

questions.text: Among the tablets recovered from Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh, which famous literary work was found in a nearly complete copy?

answers.text: The Code of Hammurabi
The Sumerian King List
The Epic of Gilgamesh
The Behistun Inscription

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This connects Ashurbanipal's library, over a thousand years later, back to one of this course's very first Primary Sources in Week 2.

questions.text: What happened to the city of Nineveh in 612 BC?

answers.text: It was besieged for roughly three months, fell, and was destroyed, never again serving as an imperial capital
It repelled the siege and remained Assyria's capital for centuries afterward
It was peacefully abandoned with no siege at all
It became the new capital of the Median Empire

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Nineveh's fall marks the effective end of the Neo-Assyrian Empire.

questions.text: What material and technique are especially associated with the construction of Babylon's Ishtar Gate under Nebuchadnezzar II?

answers.text: Glazed blue brick with sculpted bulls and dragons
Unpainted mudbrick
Solid gold plating
Carved wooden panels

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Nebuchadnezzar's own building inscriptions, a Primary Source from this course, describe this construction directly.

questions.text: What happened to Jerusalem in 586 BC?

answers.text: It was peacefully absorbed into the Babylonian Empire with no destruction
It became fully independent of all outside powers
It was destroyed along with its Temple, and its population deported, beginning the Babylonian exile
It was rebuilt as Nebuchadnezzar's new imperial capital

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This event sets up the later Persian-era return this course studied in Week 17.

questions.text: In what region did the Medes make their homeland, in the centuries before they rose to imperial power?

answers.text: The Nile Delta
The Anatolian coast
The Arabian desert
The Zagros Mountains, east of Mesopotamia

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This mountainous homeland helps explain why Median power took centuries to become visible to the empires further west.

questions.text: What unusual event, in 585 BC, is said to have interrupted a war between Media and Lydia?

answers.text: A sudden famine across both kingdoms
A solar eclipse during battle that unnerved both armies
A surprise alliance between Lydia and Assyria
The death of both kings on the same day

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This event, known as the Battle of the Eclipse, is one of the few ancient battles historians can date with real astronomical precision.

questions.text: The legendary founding stories of Carthage (Dido) and Rome (Romulus and Remus) share which key similarity?

answers.text: Both cities were founded by the same person
Both legends describe exile, hardship, and a small, uncertain settlement, with neither founder aware of what the city would eventually become
Both cities were founded on exactly the same calendar date
Both legends were written down by the same ancient author

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This pattern echoes the same foundling-hero contingency this course first met with Sargon in Week 3.

questions.text: What technological thread continued to spread even during Greece's impoverished Dark Age, when long-distance Bronze Age trade routes had broken down?

answers.text: Papyrus manufacturing
Chariot warfare
Monumental palace construction
Ironworking, since iron ore could be found and worked locally without the collapsed tin trade

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This continuity ties back to the Hittites' own ironworking, spotlighted earlier in Week 8.

questions.text: Around 550 BC, Cyrus of Persia took which action that founded the Achaemenid Empire?

answers.text: He conquered Egypt outright
He revolted against his overlord Astyages, uniting Media and Persia under his own rule
He founded the Achaemenid Empire as a co-ruler alongside Darius I
He orchestrated the fall of Babylon

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: This is the founding act behind everything Cyrus and his successors accomplished afterward.

questions.text: How did Babylon fall to Cyrus's forces in 539 BC?

answers.text: After a ten-year siege, similar to Tyre's
With remarkably little resistance, amid the Babylonian priesthood's discontent with King Nabonidus
Through a naval blockade of the Euphrates River
Only after Cyrus's own death

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: Cyrus's reputation for tolerance, expressed in the Cyrus Cylinder, is closely tied to how this conquest unfolded.

questions.text: What happened at the Battle of Pelusium in 525 BC?

answers.text: Egypt successfully repelled the Persian invasion
A peace treaty was signed and no fighting occurred
Assyria intervened militarily on Egypt's behalf
Cambyses's Persian army decisively defeated Psamtik III, ending Egypt's independent royal tradition

questions.feedback_general: Correct answer explanation: For the first time in this course's story, Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Persia's homeland all answered to a single empire.

quizzes.title: R.5 Course Reflection: Looking Back Across Eighteen Weeks

questions.text: Essential question, revisited: What made an ancient empire last, and what made one collapse? Back in this course's early weeks you may have had a first guess at this question. Now that you have studied Sargon, Hammurabi, the Bronze Age Collapse, Assyria, Babylon, and Cyrus's Persia, answer it again in three to five sentences, drawing on at least one specific example from this course.
How confident do you feel that you could explain, to someone who has never taken this course, the overall order of events from the first farming villages to Cambyses's conquest of Egypt?

answers.text: 1 = Not confident at all
2 = A little confident
3 = Somewhat confident
4 = Confident
5 = Very confident

questions.text: What is one topic, figure, or event from this course that still feels unclear to you, or that you would want to understand better? There is no wrong answer, including "nothing, I feel good about all of it."
Looking back across the rulers and events you studied in this course, which virtue do you think mattered most to the outcomes you studied?

answers.text: Courage (facing battle, siege, or a hard decision without certainty of success)
Prudence (judging correctly what a situation actually calls for)
Justice (ruling fairly, or dealing fairly with a defeated people)
Temperance (restraint, especially by a ruler with the power to go further than he did)

questions.text: Explain briefly why you chose the virtue you did in the previous question. Name the specific ruler, people, or event from this course you are thinking of.

discussions.title: 2.10 Discussion: Why Cities? The First City at Uruk
discussions.html:
Prompt: This week's lessons point to several reasons Uruk grew into a true city rather than staying a large farming village: the need to coordinate shared irrigation canals, the temple's role organizing and redistributing grain and labor, and the rise of workers who no longer farmed at all. Make a specific claim: which one of these factors do you think mattered most to Uruk actually becoming a city? Explain your reasoning, using at least one specific detail from this week's lessons or Primary Sources.

Then respond to one classmate's post. Do you agree that the factor they chose mattered most, or do you think a different factor mattered more? If you agree, strengthen their claim with an additional piece of evidence. If you disagree, respectfully explain which factor you think mattered more and why.

discussions.title: 4.10 Discussion: Hammurabi's Code
discussions.html:
Prompt: This week's lessons argue that the Code of Hammurabi offered real, predictable, publicly known justice while also building real inequality directly into its structure, both truths at once. Make a specific claim: taken as a whole, do you think the Code was more just than unjust, or more unjust than just? Support your claim by citing at least one actual law from the Code, by its number or its content.

Then respond to one classmate's post. Do you agree that the law they cited supports the conclusion they drew from it? If you agree, strengthen their claim with a different law that points the same way. If you disagree, cite a different law that complicates or challenges their claim.

discussions.title: 9.10 Discussion: The Sea Peoples and the End of an Age
discussions.html:
Prompt: This week's lessons offer several explanations for the Bronze Age Collapse: drought and famine, internal political failure, disrupted trade networks, and a combination of these factors reinforcing each other, what historians call systems collapse. Make a specific claim: which explanation do you find most convincing as the biggest factor behind the collapse? Support your claim with at least one specific detail from Ramesses III's Medinet Habu inscription or the Pylos rower tablets.

Then respond to one classmate's post. Do you agree that the cause they chose was the most important one, or does a different cause seem to explain more of what happened? If you agree, add a further piece of evidence. If you disagree, respectfully explain which cause you think mattered more and why.

discussions.title: 11.10 Discussion: From Small Kingdoms to a New Empire
discussions.html:
Prompt: Lesson 1 raises a question it does not fully answer: whether terror alone, the kind of deliberate, publicized violence Ashurnasirpal II used, can bind a large, multi-ethnic empire together over the long run, not just win individual battles. Make a specific claim: can terror alone build an empire that lasts, or does it eventually fail without something else to hold people together? Support your claim with at least one specific detail from Ashurnasirpal II's Annals or from Jehu's tribute on the Black Obelisk.

Then respond to one classmate's post. Do you agree with their claim about what terror can or cannot accomplish on its own? If you agree, strengthen their argument with an additional piece of evidence. If you disagree, respectfully explain where you think their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: 13.10 Discussion: The Ishtar Gate and the Babylonian Exile
discussions.html:
Prompt: This week tells two very different stories about lasting power. Nebuchadnezzar built the Ishtar Gate and the Etemenanki out of glazed brick and stone, meant to dazzle and endure for centuries. At the very same time, Israelite identity survived decades of exile in Babylon with no king, no temple, and no homeland at all. Make a specific claim: which form of "lasting," a monument built to impress, or a belief and identity carried by a scattered people, do you think proved more durable in this week's story? Support your claim with a specific detail from this week's lessons or Primary Sources.

Then respond to one classmate's post. Do you agree with the form of "lasting" they chose, or does the evidence point the other way to you? If you agree, strengthen their claim with an additional piece of evidence. If you disagree, respectfully explain where you think their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: 16.10 Discussion: Homer and the Memory of a Lost World
discussions.html:
Prompt: For roughly three centuries after the Mycenaean palaces fell, Greece had no writing at all, yet detailed stories about a war fought generations earlier survived anyway, carried by storytellers passing them down from memory alone, long before Homer's poems were ever written down. Make a specific claim: how reliable do you think oral tradition, memory passed down with no writing at all, actually is as a way of preserving real history? Support your claim with a specific detail from this week's lessons about how the Iliad or the Odyssey took shape.

Then respond to one classmate's post. Do you agree with how reliable, or unreliable, they judged oral tradition to be? If you agree, strengthen their claim with an additional piece of evidence. If you disagree, respectfully explain where you think their reasoning falls short.

discussions.title: R.3 Optional Course Review: Tier 2 Discussion
discussions.html:
Prompt: Which civilization's fate in this course felt least inevitable to you, and why? Choose one specific turning point from anywhere in this course, Sargon's rise, the Bronze Age Collapse, the fall of Nineveh, Cyrus's conquest of Babylon, or any other you found compelling, and make a specific claim about how easily things could have gone differently. Support your claim with at least one piece of evidence from this course's lessons or Primary Sources.

Then respond to one classmate's post. Do you agree that the moment they chose was genuinely uncertain, or do you think the outcome they describe was more likely than they suggest? If you agree, strengthen their argument with an additional piece of evidence. If you disagree, respectfully explain where you think their reasoning falls short.
